#5726. Scout Steps Toward Mass Production, With 200,000+ Reservations On The Line

Scout Motors, the revived American brand now focused on off-road capable and affordable electric trucks and SUVs, has apparently produced its first validation build vehicles at its factory in South Carolina. This is a significant step forward toward mass production for the Volkswagen Group subsidiary.

We’ve seen many EV startups come and go, including ones that revived old, historic car brands — like Detroit Electric. However, in this case, Scout is 1) offering something unique on the market, 2) focused on affordability combined with usefulness, 3) backed by automotive giant Volkswagen Group, and 4) currently has more than 200,000 reservations on the books! Reportedly, there are 212,000+ reservations for Scout EVs.

Oh, also, the company has a $2 billion factory in South Carolina, and it’s real. I’m sure there’s a lot to do there to get it filled out and operating as desired, but getting to factory production of validation build vehicles is a notable achievement that implies we are fairly close to getting actual production vehicles delivered to customers. The validation builds are of the Traveler SUV and Terra pickup truck.

The company is now able to do stamping, welding, and painting at the factory in Blythewood, South Carolina, and CEO Scott Keogh says the factory is actually 85% complete already.

After validation builds, the next phase will be pre-production vehicles. Keogh forecasts that actual production of consumer cars will begin in 2027, and deliveries will then commence in 2028. (So, customer vehicle production must be slated for the end of next year.) Construction on the factory began in 2023.

Scout was initially only going to produce 100% electric vehicles. However, it pivoted to also producing extended-range electric vehicles (vehicles that always run on electricity from a battery but whose battery can be recharged from a gas engine while driving). According to the company, 87% of those 212,000+ reservations are for the range-extended versions of the Traveler and Terra. Buyers are also heavily favoring the SUV, the Traveler, which has pulled in 75% of the reservations so far.

Keogh thinks the company could reach 400,000 reservations by the time it starts producing customer vehicles. It was at 160,000 in March and 50,000 in January. The factory is supposed to have an annual production capacity of 200,000. Having reservations for two years worth of production would be a strong, helpful boost for the company.

All of that said, one warning on the reservation tally is it has one of the same issues as the Tesla Cybertruck had — reservations are fully refundable and only cost $100. That makes it very hard to know how many people will actually go ahead and buy the vehicles once they are on offer. We will see.

#5725. People and Vertical AI: The responsible and trusted framework for energy and water

Where AI in energy and water goes next and the principles that should guide it

I have always held a simple conviction — energy and water utilities should not be spectators to the AI transformation of their own industry. They should shape it, together with the partners and technologists building alongside them.

That conviction matters because few industries carry the weight that energy and water do. They are the services every other part of modern life is built on — be it homes, hospitals, schools, businesses, data centers and increasingly, the AI economy itself. When they work, they are invisible. When they fail, everything else stops. Their success is measured in three outcomes the public feels directly: affordability, reliability and trust.

Rising energy costs, extreme weather, electrification and the growing demand from large loads are putting these outcomes under increasing pressure. At the same time, utilities are being asked to modernize operations, make better use of data and respond faster to changing customer and grid demands.

This is changing the conversation around AI. The question is no longer simply what AI can do, but where it can deliver value, how much autonomy it should have and what safeguards must govern its use.

At this year's WE3 Global AI Summit, conversations among energy and utility leaders reflected this shift. As AI moves from individual applications into customer, workforce, business and grid operations, the industry must think beyond capability to the conditions under which AI can be trusted to act.

My belief is that the answer lies in People + Vertical AI: an approach that combines industry-specific intelligence with human experience, judgment and accountability. Vertical AI brings the data, domain knowledge and operational context required to work within the realities of energy and water. People establish its purpose, define its boundaries and remain accountable for its outcomes. Four principles should guide this approach.

The relationship between customers and the grid is changing. For decades, customer service and grid operations largely functioned as separate domains. Electric vehicles, rooftop solar, battery storage and smart thermostats are increasingly connecting them. A customer's electric vehicle can become a flexible grid resource. A utility interaction about energy usage or payments can open the door to demand response and affordability programs.

This creates an opportunity for utilities to coordinate flexible demand across homes and businesses, manage peak consumption and make better use of distributed energy resources. When designed well, these programs can help defer infrastructure investments, improve grid flexibility and manage costs. But technology alone will not make this possible. Customers need clear choices, fair incentives and confidence in how their data and participation are used.

Utilities will increasingly need to manage the grid with their customers, not simply deliver services to them. Vertical AI must therefore connect the customer experience with grid intelligence, bringing these traditionally separate functions into a more coordinated operating model.

In energy and water, intelligence is not just a model. It depends on people, processes, data and security working together. When these elements remain disconnected, AI has a narrower view of utility operations and a weaker foundation for sound decisions. Yet customer, workforce, business and grid operations continue to rely on systems and data that were often designed independently. The result is fragmented information, disconnected workflows and limited visibility across the ecosystem.

This is why the real unit of value in Vertical AI is the connected workflow and this is where depth of industry data becomes decisive. It requires intelligence grounded in the industry's operating context, including utility-specific data, processes, regulatory requirements and historical interactions.

With more than 15 years of experience building Vertical AI for energy and water, we have seen how important this industry context is. Our work at SEW.AI, drawing on more than 4.3 trillion data points across energy and water usage, customer interactions and utility operations. That depth is what allows it to reason across all four domains with genuine context, connecting the systems utilities already run without replacing them.

Agentic AI moves intelligence from recommendation to execution: systems that can reason through complex, multi-step processes and carry them through to resolution.

In utilities, however, action demands specialization. A general-purpose agent can follow instructions, but it cannot be expected to grasp the regulatory, operational and safety consequences of its actions. Vertical agents start from a different premise. Each is purpose-designed for a specific domain, such as outage response, field dispatch, payments or customer care. Each is trained on industry data and governed by industry rules. Together they are orchestrated so that each hands off seamlessly to the next. What emerges is less a single intelligence than a coordinated team of specialists.

As distributed energy resources multiply and operational demands become more interconnected, this coordination will become increasingly important. Specialized agents can handle routine, repeatable tasks with greater consistency and speed, allowing utility employees to focus on exceptions, complex decisions and situations that require human judgment. The objective is not to automate every decision. It is to ensure that the right decisions are made with the right context, at the right time and that actions remain within clearly established boundaries.

The fourth principle underpins everything else: trust. And trust begins with security.

In energy and water, security is not an IT concern. It is a matter of public safety. Every AI agent introduced into a utility is a new identity with access to customer data, operational systems and, increasingly, physical infrastructure.

Security therefore cannot be layered on after deployment. It must be intrinsic — with verified identities, least-privilege access, auditable actions, appropriate data protection and clear escalation paths. Decisions with significant safety, financial or operational consequences require controls proportionate to their risk, including human approval where necessary. Governance must also extend beyond deployment. Utilities need visibility into how AI systems operate, the permissions they exercise, the decisions they influence and the circumstances in which they must escalate to people.

Governance of this kind is not a brake on innovation. It is what allows autonomy to scale responsibly, earned workflow by workflow, with accountability that always remains human. Regulators, boards and communities will hold utilities, not algorithms, responsible for every outcome.

Vertical AI brings industry knowledge, speed and scale. People bring experience, judgment and accountability. Neither is sufficient on its own.

The energy and water industries have navigated major transitions before, from electrification to digitization. Each required more than new technology. It required changes in how organizations operated, how people worked and how services were delivered to communities.

AI will demand the same discipline. Its progress should not be measured by how many decisions can be automated or how much autonomy a system can achieve. It should be measured by whether utilities can use it responsibly to make essential services more affordable, more reliable and more trusted.

That is the standard we should hold ourselves to as an industry. And it is the principle behind the People + Vertical AI approach we continue to advance.

SEW.AI is the global Vertical AI Platform purpose-built for the energy and utility industry, enabling organizations to transform customer engagement, workforce productivity, business operations and grid intelligence through the People + Vertical AI framework.

#5722. A Radically Different Approach to AI

About forty years ago, I decided I would develop artificial intelligence in my spare time. I knew about the Turing test, and I believed that a computer tricking people into thinking it was human did not indicate intelligence. There was a program called ELIZA that did that already, and it was clearly not intelligent at all.

I wanted to produce real AI, a type of thought that might take some effort for a human being to figure out. Maybe I would have to ask the computer how it reached the conclusion it did. But it would do so using logic a human could follow, examining each step. It would be a process a person could examine.

My goal, I believed, would best be reached by first inventing something I called Artificial Cognition. This would be a native way for computers to deal with data in the form of bit-fields, which were native data for computers, as translations of human words, in the same way that computers use IEEE bitwise representations of real numbers. Once this step was done, it would be easy to string words together in sentences, which could be directly translated into and out of human language. And the sentences would tell computers things they could “understand.”

With such translations, a computer could translate a work, such as Shakespeare’s Henry V, into its own language. Then it could translate the text into whatever language we might want. Some subtleties would be lost, but human translators do the same thing.

My idea was that computers should be able to work on ideas natively. At first, I thought this would require a very wide CPU, with registers that might be 256 bits, or even wider. In time, I came to believe that it would be best to stick to CPUs that were in use. As 64-bit CPUs were clearly coming soon, when I was working on this in 1986, I decided to use that data size. I also thought I might have to design a CPU with an additional instruction set, but I never got to the point of needing one.

So my design goal ended up having a word to translate almost any word (or even phrases) of English, occupying 64 bits of memory. And these could be understood and manipulated in standard registers of a standard computer.

I believe that I did achieve that goal, though the project never went into commercial use. A patent on the final design was issued by the US PTO, but that was long ago, and as I understand it, the whole thing is now in the public domain.

My reason for writing about this is that AI is a very contentious issue today. Anthropic has even warned potential stockholders in its IPO documents that its product could have catastrophic effects if things go wrong, possibly to the point of terminating all human life. I think it even points out that a major part of the value of its stock would be lost if there were no human beings left to buy it.

So I started to work on what I called Artificial Cognition in about 1986. Doing this in my spare time was a long slog. I went through a bunch of design iterations, starting, as I said, with 256-bit words. I won’t go through the work that had to be done determining how many designs there were and why each would not work. Each attempt took about a year or more, but eventually I got to the point of having a design in my fifth try.

I will give a simple explanation of the design in this article. Before I do, I will describe what the design could do at the time the patent was applied for, over twenty years ago. To reiterate, it could do these things:

Eventually, I defined about 10,000 words for this design. Doing this was a full-time project that took two years, during which I also tested the design. At a point where I had about 2,500 words, I built a simple program that took two inputs of English words, translated them into the computer words, compared them to see that they were valid for compares, and held them for the record. Then it went through the entire vocabulary, taking each word (or set of words) in turn and finding any word that compared to it in precisely the same way the first two words compared.

This might sound like it did far more work than it needed to do. Because most words are not comparable, most compares produced faults and were rejected immediately. So the process did not have to do the millions of compares one might imagine. This was even easier than one might suppose, because whole huge sets of words could be rejected together. So if the input words were a pair like “train” and “airplane,” all words for colors or pieces of clothing could be rejected as sets.

One thing about this that is interesting is how it is done in the computer CPU. With a pair of 64-bit registers loaded, an XOR instruction will result in the difference between the two, or it will produce a fault. The XOR requires a single clock cycle. Then, with the word from the dictionary loaded into a register, a single XOR with the difference produces the word that gives the analogy, or it will produce a fault.

If there is a fault, we go on to the next word in the vocabulary. Otherwise, we have an analogy. In practice, for example, I ran this using original inputs of “car” and “small passenger plane.” The results came back, including the examples following, for “as a car is to a small passenger plane” (please note that each set of words in quotes is a single 64-bit word for the computer):

There were many other results, but the combination of lion and eagle stood out so clearly that I looked specifically to see what the comparison entailed. Why “lion” and “eagle,” but not “tiger” and “owl,” or “house cat” and “hawk”? There were about half a dozen predatory land animals and at least four predatory birds in that small dictionary, but “lion” and “eagle” were the only pair returned by the program. What gives?

It turned out that things had gone precisely the way they should have. The reason that “lion” and “eagle” were chosen while others were not is that the definitions of these two had connotative values as symbols of authority. That information was in their 64-bit definitions. You can do a lot with 64 bits, if you know how.

This work was done in a 32-bit machine, simulating the 64-bit machines just about to come to market. With registers loaded (in a 64-bit machine), each compare would take one clock cycle. So the whole thing, with computers pre-loaded, would take two clocks. In a 2-GHz machine, the set of compares took one billionth of a second. One billionth of a second in a 64-bit machine anyone could buy. One billionth of a second in a Raspberry Pi costing $45.

AI companies are bringing products to market that they warn could end the lives of all human beings. Anthropic says its IPO, which comes out on Thursday, will establish the value of the company at $1.5 trillion (NOTE: with a “T”). But Anthropic is warning that a risk for stockholders is that it could kill all humanity, including you, and your entire family, even if you live in a modest home and get no benefit from the company in any way. And everyone else could go with you. That, I read, is what the IPO papers say, but some people believe it could be very worthwhile to do.

I believe this is not artificial intelligence. It might be artificial neglect. Maybe even artificial willful ignorance. Maybe, with artificial rational thought, we could produce artificial due diligence, but AI is not known for rationality.

I wonder how high the value of Anthropic stock will go if only computers could buy it because there were no people left. Of course, without a Fed made up of humans, they might figure out a way to have infinite money to play with.

The iteration of my invention that works depends on 64 bits being divided into categories, each represented by 8 bits. These are organized into eight supersets (3 bits), each with four groups of subsets (2 bits), with each group having eight basic subsets (3 bits). The total is 8 bits per set value, so there are 256 categories.

Of the eight supersets in each category, one is “agent.” This is anything that does anything. It is divided into four groups of subsets, two of which are “living thing” and “mechanism.” These are divided by type into subsets, so “living thing” includes “animal” and “plant,” among others.

The category “location and time” is similar. This is divided into groups of subsets, one of which is “geography.” Within this are eight subsets, among which are “air,” “land,” “water,” “space,” and four others.

We can see the basic way the vocabulary works by taking these for the most significant 8 bits in a word, the field I call “BAS,” and the next most significant field, which I call “ALT,” because I seem to be unable to come up with a better 3-letter name for it. (Sorry, I do get a bit dull sometimes. Often.)

Using just these two fields, we can see that a car, a train, a taxi, a bus, and a bicycle are all in a group, “land vehicle” (for ALT and BAS). An airplane of any type is an “air vehicle.” So are a blimp and a kite carrying prayers to the clouds asking them to make rain.

Similarly, a lion, tiger, bear, or dog would be a “land animal,” and most birds are “air animal.” Please note that I say “most birds.” They are not divided into biological groups, but according to where they function. Some birds only function on land. Similarly, a bat is an “air animal.” And Melville was right, Moby Dick was a “water animal,” just like any fish.

This broadly divides our dictionary into potential word values using 16 bits. This would limit us to just 65,536 potential words, if they were 16 bits long. Fortunately, we are only a quarter of the way through the 64 bits of our potential word definitions.

The next parts of the definition use 8 bits for each of several fields. A SRC field could represent where something comes from, why it has come into existence, or even what fuels it. For a car, this could be a value that decodes as “chemical,” or a value meaning “electricity.” For a sail-powered car, this field might mean “air.” For just “car,” with no motive force specified, this would be left to the value 0, meaning “any” or “whatever.”

An MTD field represents how it is operated. For a car, this could be decoded by a word meaning “engine” or “motor.” That is, unless the car is powered by sail, in which case neither of these values would work, but something other than 0 would be used, because 0 could mean a superset that engines and motors would match to. In the case of a buggy, this field would say “animal.”

A DST field may mean a destination or purpose. For a car, this could be a value meaning “human being,” for what it carries.

In addition to these, there is a CXT field, which can carry context. In the case of a lion or eagle, this is a value meaning “authority,” which is why they matched to each other but nothing else in the test.

So far, I have described six fields. They provide us with far more potential words than any human language has by a huge factor. That should be enough, but there are other uses for bits. For example, I decided some time ago that there should be eight bits assigned to negation bits, each corresponding to a single field in the word.

Clearly, the values that make up the fields in the word are very fuzzy in their meanings. However, in the design, applying how these are to be interpreted has to be done strictly according to the sets of words involved. Implementing such a design means rules have to be developed according what part of the vocabulary is being worked on.

Altogether, I had a bit over 10,000 words defined about twenty years ago. I believed that these could be built up just a bit for software that could read a dictionary. As it happened, no one was willing to look at the invention to evaluate it, so funding of my invention ceased.

Before I finish up, I should mention that this sort of AI does not do images or other types of jobs that require pattern matching. That isn’t what I set out to do. I always assumed that such things would come from people interested in them. But I wasn’t interested.

I have a problem with the AI being produced commercially today. All of it looks to me like it is based on the same sort of pattern matching that is done by a human mind to some extent. And this is a problem because human beings are not naturally rational creatures. So AI companies are basically building irrational products.

As for Anthropic and the other organizations that claim to have products that threaten human life, that looks like artificial insanity requiring artificial restraint. Or artificial constraint. At least until someone can develop artificial ethics and artificial caution. I don’t think Anthropic has that yet. But I think there is a way to do it.

#5721. SOLRITE and sonnen collaborate on integrated VPP breaker

SOLRITE and sonnen plan to digitally integrate VPP smart breakers into what the companies are calling the SOLRITE sonnen VPP. The expanded VPP Node combines sonnenHub with ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart breaker technology to manage major household loads. The VPP smart breaker, controlled by ADAPT Energy, can also participate in on-grid VPP events, enabling the same electrical infrastructure to be used for both backup and grid participation.

“Our work with ADAPT Energy is a meaningful step forward in how we think about residential battery storage and VPP participation,” said Regan George, CEO and founder of SOLRITE Energy. “We have already demonstrated the tremendous value of connecting sonnen batteries together as a pooled grid asset. Now, we’re going inside the home and unlocking another layer of flexibility that has been sitting there all along. By combining the battery with additional load management made possible by the VPP smart breaker technology, we’re creating a more valuable node for the grid while also giving homeowners a clever backup solution.”

The system can shed large loads without requiring those circuits to be relocated. ADAPT Energy keeps the smart breakers synchronized with the sonnen battery during backup mode and automatically restores the breakers when grid power returns.

This integration is designed to manage whole-home electrical loads in the background, not requiring homeowners to reset circuits during an outage.

“This is about making whole-home backup work the way homeowners expect it to,” said Troy Morgan, president of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy. “Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired, and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home. Our technology empowers home loads to supply optimal backup power during an outage or provide valuable flexibility to the grid.”

When a VPP event happens, the sonnen battery can discharge or charge with direct load shedding via ADAPT. ADAPT Energy will strictly shed pre-approved household loads. A customer who has opted to include a pool pump, for example, can have that load temporarily turned off while the sonnen battery is discharging to the grid.

“With the addition of ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart-breaker technology to the SOLRITE–sonnen ecosystem, we are expanding the virtual power plant from a battery-centered resource into a fully orchestrated home-energy platform,” said Blake Richetta, chairman and CEO of sonnen. “By synchronizing energy that has been harnessed in our battery with intelligent, real-time control of household electrical loads, we can deliver more flexible, responsive capacity to the grid precisely when it is needed most. This integration materially strengthens the value of SOLRITE’s virtual power plant—supporting grid reliability, creating greater customer value, and enabling SOLRITE to continue delivering industry-leading solar-plus-storage VPA solutions to homeowners.”

#5720. Over court objections, DOE issues 7th order to keep Michigan coal plant online

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Environmental groups say they are “evaluating all legal options” after a federal appeals court vacated a previous order for the same plant, ruling DOE exceeded its authority.

Utility Dive reported in June that Campbell was operating at a capacity factor of 46.1%, down from a nearly 66% average in the same periods in the previous four years.

Environmental and consumer advocates say there is no energy emergency requiring the plant to remain online, and forcing it to stay active has already saddled consumers with excess costs.

Consumers spent $303 million through the end of September to operate the plant under DOE emergency orders after accounting for $344 million in market revenues, according to its quarterly filing.

Consumers spokesperson Brian Wheeler said the utility “will continue to follow the law and operate our Campbell plant,” and that “consistent with these emergency orders, we will work to ensure that everyone who benefits from power from the Campbell plant across the Midwest pays their fair share.”

“Someone will be left holding the financial bag,” ELPC CEO Howard Learner said in a statement. And following the appeals court decision, the “latest purported emergency order is likewise illegal.”

“DOE should just stop issuing these orders and stop the meter from running up costs,” he said.

DOE did not immediately respond to questions about the new order and what may happen next.

The latest order will keep the 1,420-MW plant online another 90 days, until mid-February, bringing the total extension to more than 20 months, according to the Environmental Defense Fund.

Meanwhile, Consumers is seeking to recover “ballooning costs” from ratepayers in 11 states, EDF said: Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota and Wisconsin.

Campbell “illustrates the enormous price tag attached to keeping these uneconomic coal plants on life support for months on end,” Ted Kelly, EDF director and lead counsel for U.S. clean energy, said in a statement. “These are completely unnecessary costs, yet families and businesses that are already stretched thin are being asked to foot the bill.”

According to DOE, coal plants across the U.S. “are being saved from premature retirement,” and in 2025 more than 17 GW of coal-fired electricity generation was preserved.

The J.H. Campbell power plant had been set to retire in May 2025. Ensuring Campbell and other coal plants are available to operate “has prevented blackouts and likely saved lives,” Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in DOE’s latest announcement.

The emergency conditions that led to the issuance of the original order persist, the agency said, and a joint report from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the North American Electric Reliability Corporation and NERC’s Regional Entities “highlights how events that occurred during the Winter 2026 Arctic Cold Period, including Winter Storm Fern, demonstrated the need for dispatchable generation capacity from facilities like the Campbell Plant.”

According to EDF, since May 2025 the Trump administration has “repeatedly extended emergency orders to keep six coal plants online beyond retirement, even as those plants have racked up around $600 million in losses.”

“Of the unlawfully extended coal plants, the Campbell plant in Michigan has emitted the most health-harming air pollution,” it added.

According to the Michigan League of Conservation Voters, DOE’s latest order to keep Campbell open “will eat away at more than half of the $600 million the plant’s closure was set to save Michiganders by 2040.”

Consumers in Michigan “deserve affordable energy and relief from rising costs — not executive overreach that forces families to subsidize aging, expensive fossil fuel infrastructure,” Bentley Johnson, federal government affairs director for Michigan LCV, said in a statement.

#5718. NAED Unveils PV-1 PECVD-V, a U.S.-Engineered Vertical Deposition Platform Built for 96,000-Wafer-per-Hour Tandem Solar Manufacturing

Patent-pending vertical PECVD/PVD architecture doubles wafer throughput over NAED’s previous platform and is designed to produce perovskite/HJT tandem cells targeting 30% efficiency

NAED Energy Holding Inc. (“NAED”), the U.S. aerospace, engineering, and utility-energy company behind NAED Nexus Core™, last week unveiled PV-1 PECVD-V, a vertical in-line deposition platform for high-volume solar cell manufacturing. PV-1 combines plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) and physical vapor deposition (PVD) on a single shared-carrier line. It is designed for a throughput of 96,000 wafers per hour, double the 48,000 wafers per hour of NAED’s previous XL-class platform.

In PV-1, wafers travel upright on a shared carrier through every PECVD and PVD stage. To reach the second side of the wafer, the system never flips the substrate: the entire carrier is lifted and turned 180 degrees as a unit. This keeps wafers seated in the same carrier from first deposition to last, cutting direct wafer handling between process steps. The PV-1 production line, its 180-degree carrier turn, its wafer-retention carrier, and the T2X tandem cell are the subject of pending U.S. patent applications assigned to NAED Energy Holding Inc. NAED’s intellectual property portfolio has been independently appraised at $179 million under an ASC 820 Level 3 fair-value methodology, as of November 11, 2026.

PV-1 was engineered from the start for tandem solar. The full line, including perovskite top-cell process tools, is designed to produce NAED’s T2X two-terminal perovskite/heterojunction (HJT) tandem cell, which targets 30% cell efficiency. NAED plans to bring T2X cells to both terrestrial and space solar markets, alongside a family of glass-glass T2X modules starting at 600 W.

Every PV-1 tool is designed in-house by NAED and machined in its own aerospace-grade CNC shop in the United States. The first six of PV-1’s thirteen process tools are complete, and the remaining seven are in production. Engineering and design for the full PV-1 line and its production facility are complete.

“Going vertical, let us double throughput and build the line around tandem cells from day one, rather than retrofitting tandem onto a platform designed for something else,” said Malcom Longair, Media & Development Lead, NAED Energy Holding Inc. “With PV-1, manufacturers anywhere in the world can reserve U.S.-engineered deposition equipment built for the next generation of solar cells.”

NAED is now opening reservations for PV-1 production tool slots to solar cell manufacturers in the United States and internationally. Manufacturers can request specifications and reserve a slot at NAED. energy or through the media and partnership contact below.

News release from NAED Energy Holding, Inc.

#5716. FERC’s See on large loads, Western markets and affordability

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

FERC’s Lindsay See on federal permitting reform: “I think one of the biggest drivers in terms of cost and extra time is uncertainty in legal statutes.”

Lindsay See, a member of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission since mid-2024, has been a leader on the agency’s permitting reform initiatives and has joined other commissioners in pushing transmission owners to use grid-enhancing technologies. Utility Dive met with See on Wednesday at the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners’ annual meeting in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Before joining FERC, See served as West Virginia’s solicitor general, where she successfully argued a case at the U.S. Supreme Court challenging greenhouse gas rules for power plants.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

LINDSAY SEE: I find NARUC really valuable because I am a former state attorney myself. I worked for the West Virginia [attorney general’s] office. I firmly believe in the importance of state and local solutions, and I think that's what I want to say to the states.

But primarily, it's what I want to hear from the states because I think we have so many issues where we have jurisdiction at FERC, and the states do, [too,] and I want to make sure that we're pulling in the same direction. So that's a lot of my message: How do we keep lines of communication open so they have the information they need from us, and vice versa.

I want to learn the different ways that states are approaching affordability issues, large-load challenge issues, how we can help at FERC. Some of what we're looking at is, how do we make sure that a lot of these new regulatory pushes and policies we have don't have unintended consequences.

They want more transparency, especially when it's coming to affordability issues. How do we make sure that they have the same information that we have so that they can do their job better when it comes to allocating retail rates? Particularly when it comes to large-load integration, there's been some blind spots on the state side in terms of which customers on the transmission side are driving those costs.

Even just a few years ago, when I worked in West Virginia, we didn't talk about PJM that much. Now we have regular ratepayers who are not energy nerds who are reading about PJM on the front page of the news and are seeing their bills go higher. So I think we're seeing a lot more pressure on what we're doing to understand, what do we have responsibility over, what don't we? That kind of public conversation is really different, but really helpful because it puts a really important focus for us to make sure that we have a clear sense of what we can control and what we can't control.

We've got a few buckets that we're really focused on. One is — especially when it comes to large-load integration and the show cause orders we have — how do we have transmission cost agreements that are clear about which customers are driving those costs to make sure that they're the ones who are paying their share and we're not saddling existing customers with those costs or with the risk of stranded investment.

In order to meet this incredible opportunity we have from large-load growth as a country, it's going to take new transmission investment that's absolutely required and it's necessarily expensive. So I think it's even more important for us to make sure that we are making the right sort of investments into the system.

In those show-cause orders, we focused on requiring transmission owners to consider alternative transmission technologies — to say, how can we do more with the existing system. I'm really focused on pushing as far as we can within our statutory structure because I understand we need new wires. But I want to make sure we've got the right incentives in place to use what we already have really well.

We need more infrastructure, both on the transmission side and on the pipeline side, so how do we make that permitting process as efficient and streamlined as possible? Because reducing that time and the legal uncertainty also has a direct cost consequence in terms of the amount of money those projects ultimately cost. So that is something within our control in areas where we've got permitting authority.

We see so much of the electricity sector that's powered by natural gas, being able to get that fuel where it needs to be at the right time is critical in order to have a reliable and affordable electricity sector, too. So the way I look at it is, everything that we can do to encourage a more efficient, streamlined, legally durable permitting process on the gas side has direct consequences on the power side, too.

I hear those concerns. I take them seriously. I, probably unsurprisingly, disagree with them. We do have really important environmental responsibilities, [and] I think it matters for us to fulfill those, but also not to go further than what the statutes require. And so I think some of the work that we've been doing over the past year and just in the past month, announcing a new draft policy statement, is really trying to be clear about where that line of what we're required to do begins and ends.

[The National Environmental Policy Act] is a statute that affirmatively requires us to create evidence in terms of the environmental record, but it doesn't require particular types of evidence.

So when we come to air modeling, for instance … my view is, we're not the environmental regulators and experts. EPA and the states are already doing a lot of that work, so we should be able to take advantage of the good work they're doing. There's other evidence that is not so time-intensive and kind of fraught with legal uncertainty and vulnerability that lets us do our particular job.

When anyone is putting information in the record, we are still required to consider that in the public interest. So we're not turning a blind eye to those concerns at all. This is just about what particular evidence we are specifically required to create. So I think not having redundancies in terms of what other agencies do, it doesn't take away from our responsibilities.

I am strongly supportive of permitting reform. I'm a former litigator. I lived in the trenches here. I think one of the biggest drivers in terms of cost and extra time is uncertainty in legal statutes when it comes to either agencies taking more time than they might need to to cover their bases. And then, of course, the time it takes in court, and if the agency loses and remands, we have to start over. That just adds so much in terms of time we, frankly, don't have to build out the system and [adds] cost to consumers.

We've been taking stock internally if this becomes law. There are huge responsibilities that FERC has in the bill, so we're trying to gear up and come up with a plan for how to do that.

PJM has significant challenges ahead. This is not a normal demand spike that we're seeing. The market was not designed for the circumstances we have with such large-load growth. And some of the PJM states are at the epicenter of data center growth.

We are seeing some reforms coming that are really targeted and focused on these urgent needs, but I think one of the things — and these are conversations I've had with PJM, and I know my colleagues have, too —  is how do we make sure it's not just playing whack-a-mole? And being able to have a vision for the future. I think the confidence piece for all market participants is so critical right now.

I think that loops back to some of the ongoing conversations about governance at PJM. We had a technical conference a few months ago where all the commissioners focused on this issue, and we're about to be getting some proposals. [The governance] issue matters a lot because in order for PJM to be nimble to respond to these concerns and to have the public's confidence, I think the governance piece is so critical to unlock the ability to move forward on some of these other substantive areas.

They get to make those decisions, and we support the choices they make. I spent a good amount of time out West last spring, and I was really encouraged to see those really collegial and thoughtful conversations in the West. They are watching very closely what's happening in the Eastern markets, too, to see what's working and what's not.

[The difficulties in PJM,] I think it's galvanizing the states out West to make sure that they're setting the right governance structures in place from the beginning that protect their voice and their interests. That's something I'm watching really closely on PJM market reform … what does it look like to have increased state involvement in the decision-making process that also corresponds to their increased responsibility for the regional issues?

I think about it in two ways. First, FERC is a creature of statute. We have our statutory mission. Permitting reform might change that, but the midterms don't. It's business as usual in that sense.

But the midterms definitely drive home how much Americans are concerned about the cost of living and about their energy bills specifically, and that goes to the heart of our mission for reliable and affordable energy. So I look at that, and I take that concern to heart. If anything, it puts a renewed focus and onus on us to make sure that when it comes to those areas within our control, we are really taking a hard look at what we can be doing.

#5714. Mobile Energy Hubs: How Chery Auto’s Smart Energy Ecosystem Supports the Development of Smart Cities Worldwide

WUHU, China — Following the 2026 Chery International User Summit, Chery Auto is pressing ahead with its new energy ecosystem strategy. Entering the Globalization 3.0 phase, the company is deploying a mix of energy solutions to meet mobility energy needs around the world. As electric vehicles integrate with power grids, Chery Auto is developing a smart energy ecosystem that transforms new energy vehicles (NEVs) into dispatchable distributed mobile energy nodes, supporting grid management, sustainable urban development, and local energy resource utilization.

Unlike conventional charging, which can increase peak demand, V2G offers a flexible alternative. Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) enables bidirectional flow, allowing vehicles to store off-peak electricity and return power during peak demand. For users, this creates opportunities to participate in energy management and potentially generate value. With participation depending on commercial feasibility and user confidence, Chery Group’s global user base exceeding 21 million provides a foundation for V2G deployment.

Chery Auto is validating its energy ecosystem across homes, communities and industrial parks. Its household Energy Cube integrates solar, storage and bidirectional charging to support electricity supply during exceptional conditions. In Wuhu, a large-scale AC V2G demonstration station enables private vehicles to support grid management through onboard chargers with limited modifications. In Spain, an industrial park microgrid uses green electricity to reduce energy costs, fossil fuel dependence, and carbon emissions.

Chery Auto’s Volt-dragon Ultra-Fast Charging technology targets 500 km of range in five minutes. Its hybrid engine has achieved 48.57% thermal efficiency, while the planned Rhino S solid-state battery targets 400 Wh/kg energy density. Chery’s Rhino Battery prioritizes fast charging, longevity and safety, addressing battery degradation and thermal management concerns associated with V2G charging cycles.

Chery Auto is developing modular solar, storage, charging, and V2G solutions tailored to regional infrastructure. In Europe, electricity markets provide opportunities for distributed energy participation. Mature markets integrate vehicles into grid management, while regions with weaker infrastructure can prioritize microgrids before introducing V2G.

Through applications spanning households, communities, and industrial parks, Chery Auto is extending automotive-grade engineering into energy infrastructure. Its approach supports distributed energy networks using locally generated electricity and managing energy flows, positioning Chery to participate in future smart cities.

#5712. NRG to sell 4.9 GW of gas plants to LS Power for $4B

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

NRG Energy CEO Robert Gaudette said the sale values one 1.2-GW Texas gas plant at $1,400/kW, while NRG is “developing 1.5 GW of new natural gas generation in Texas” for just above $1,000/kW.

NRG Energy has agreed to sell around 4.9 GW of gas plant capacity to LS Power, which approached NRG with an unsolicited offer of $4 billion — around eight times the plants’ annual adjusted EBITDA of $500 million, NRG President and CEO Robert Gaudette said during a Nov. 9 earnings call.

NRG plans for that $4 billion to go toward a $1 billion stock buyback and $2 billion debt reduction, with the remaining $1 billion providing “flexibility to reinvest in our long-term strategy through attractive contracted growth opportunities or further reduce debt,” Gaudette said. “We expect the sale to close in the second quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals.”

“One aspect of the valuation worth highlighting is Jack County, which carries an implied value of approximately $1,400/KW,” Gaudette said. “For perspective, we're developing 1.5 GW of new natural gas generation in Texas for just above $1,000/KW. That comparison demonstrates the value we're realizing from selected existing assets while developing newer, more efficient generation at a lower cost.”

Gaudette said that NRG’s project of building a 1.2-GW combined-cycle natural gas-fired power plant in Texas to power the data center project of an unnamed cloud and AI hyperscaler is “on track, and I fully expect approved agreements and an announcement by year-end.”

“We're also advancing additional project opportunities with the same customer beyond the initial 1.2 GW,” he added. “Beyond the initial project, our pipeline of opportunities exceeds the turbine allocations and [engineering, procurement, and construction] capacity under our original development agreement with GE Vernova and Kiewit.”

That development agreement is for 5.4 GW of turbine capacity, according to NRG’s earnings presentation.

In response to an analyst question about whether the results of the recent midterm elections present any risks to the 1.2-GW project, Gaudette said, “The political environment has actually strengthened this project and our projects.”

“The way that we've gone about developing generation to support data centers and this large load growth over time, the political environment is where we thought it would always be,” he added. “We've been very picky about the projects we do and very picky about who we do them with … I've actually talked to our customer since the elections. This project is going to happen.”

Gaudette noted that “prices in ERCOT are depressed,” which is built into the company’s 2027 guidance and long-term outlook, he said.

“Right now we're in a world where battery build and solar have kind of dominated the last two years of build, and demand hasn't been fast enough to absorb all of it,” he added. Gaudette called 2027 “weak,” but noted that the ERCOT region has a strong pipeline overall.

“When you look into the queue in ERCOT, it's not just data centers,” he said. “There's multiple gigawatts of manufacturing facilities, expansions of industrial facilities. Those are coming. Those have jobs. Those are going to hit the grid and sop up some of that excess capacity … NRG is very well positioned to capture value both on the retail side and the generation side as this market tightens and our customers need us more.”

#5710. COP31 Leaders’ Summit Spotlights Electrification & Transition Away from Fossil Fuels

Antalya, Türkiye — The COP31 Leaders’ Summit concluded today, with several new announcements and speeches from heads of state and the UN Secretary-General. Developments included country endorsements of the COP Presidency’s 35×35 electrification pledge, growing support for the transition away from fossil fuels, and new pledges from philanthropies to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, among others.

Following is a statement from Ani Dasgupta, President and CEO, World Resources Institute:

“One message came across loud and clear from world leaders: climate action has shifted from an environmental movement to a core economic and security imperative. The conversation is moving beyond high-level commitments to the practical challenges of how to transition away from fossil fuels while supporting workers and communities and how to put entire economies on a cleaner, more resilient path.

“Electrification and the transition away from fossil fuels rightly took center stage. These are two vital, intertwined goals, and progress on one must reinforce the other. Early support for the 35×35 electrification pledge is encouraging, but many more countries need to endorse it and turn their commitments into credible national plans backed by concrete policies and investment.

“President Lula deserves credit for keeping the transition away from fossil fuels at the top of the international agenda and delivering a global roadmap that countries can adapt to their own circumstances. Australia and Türkiye now have an opportunity to lead by example, putting forward their own transition plans and encouraging others to follow.

“Vulnerable countries delivered an equally clear message: access to affordable finance is critical to them implementing their climate ambition. High borrowing costs and unsustainable debt are holding back investment in the very countries that need it most. With the $1.3 trillion finance goal established, the focus is shifting to how all sources of finance can work together to deliver investment at scale and how we ensure affordable capital reaches those who need it most. There are encouraging signs, including an influx of pledges from philanthropies for the Brazil-initiated Tropical Forests Forever Facility.

“Adaptation and early warning systems received much-needed attention after a year of crushing heatwaves, fires, and floods. But that attention now needs to turn to the investment in systemic resilience as the best way to make economies and societies stronger and improve people’s lives. Building more resilient cities was a major focus and will take deep collaboration between national governments, cities, and states. Cities are on the front lines of delivering the climate solutions and essential services that make people’s lives better, and demonstrating these benefits is critical to accelerating the transition. Local leaders are on the front lines of climate impacts and the delivery of essential services that make communities safer, healthier, and more resilient, yet too often lack the resources to respond. Cities and local communities especially need greater access to adaptation finance.

“It was disappointing to see no dedicated ocean event at the Leaders’ Summit, despite over 90% of countries including ocean action in national climate plans. The ocean is on the front lines of the climate crisis, but it could also be one of our greatest allies in tackling it. Ocean-based solutions can provide up to one-third of the emissions cuts needed by 2050 to keep 1.5°C within reach. This ambition for ocean action must be reflected in any COP31 cover decision and translate into concrete progress, especially for vulnerable coastal and island nations.

“Some leaders also delivered a resounding defense of multilateralism, even amid deep geopolitical tensions. International cooperation on climate may be changing shape, but it is still alive and needed now more than ever. Even in a fractured world, leaders recognize that no country can secure its economic future, build resilience, or prosper without working together on shared climate and environmental challenges. That spirit of cooperation must now carry through the negotiations and deliver a strong, ambitious outcome at COP31.”

WRI is a global research organization that spans more than 50 countries, with offices in Brazil, China, Europe, India, Indonesia, and the United States. Our more than 450 experts and staff work closely with leaders to turn big ideas into action to sustain our natural resources—the foundation of economic opportunity and human well-being. Find out more at www.wri.org

#5708. Elevated demand for gas turbines could persist through 2035: Siemens Energy

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The U.S. midterms are not likely to slow turbine orders by data centers, company executives said, noting turbine demand is also coming from diverse industries with long-term growth trajectories.

Siemens Energy continues to book new orders at a record pace, with the company's backlog reaching 164 billion euros (about $180.4 billion) as of the end of the company's 2026 fiscal year, executives told analysts on a Nov. 11 earnings call.

New order intake rose 18.8% over the end of fiscal year 2025, according to the company's earnings release. The second half of the year also saw sharp increases in wind turbine sales from subsidiary Siemens Gamesa, allowing the company's offshore-wind-focused arm to break even for the first time in years, according to Siemens Energy President and CEO Christian Bruch.

“I do strongly believe in offshore ... being a decent-sized market in selected countries of the world, and that is still my underlying assumption — that we can play on the strengths we have in offshore,” Bruch said.

Gas turbine orders moderated somewhat in the fourth and final quarter of the fiscal year, but CFO Maria Ferraro attributed the slightly slower pace of orders to “project phasing.” Bruch said he does not believe that the growing data center backlash that manifest in the U.S. midterm elections has impacted demand for turbines or other electrical equipment. U.S. orders rose 70% year over year, with $6.7 billion in new orders booked during the fourth quarter alone, according to a Siemens Energy press release.

Globally, data center-related customers account for about 15 billion euros ($16.5 billion) of Siemen's backlog, Ferraro said.

“This translates to less than 10% of the total,” she told analysts. “So data centers are an important factor, and we certainly want to participate, but our growth story is much broader and very well diversified.”

Siemens Energy expects data centers to represent about a fifth of the growth in global demand for electricity, which the company expects to grow 60% by 2040. The electrification of transportation, manufacturing growth, and rising consumption of electricity within other buildings will drive the majority of new demand, Bruch said.

On top of this, he said he expects renewable energy capacity to triple by 2040, and he believes the world's most advanced nations need to replace about half of their existing electrical grid. As a result, Bruch said, orders for gas turbines should continue at roughly their current pace through 2030 — and possibly through 2035.

To meet this demand, Siemens Energy plans to invest about 4 billion euros ($4.4 billion) in manufacturing capacity by 2030, Bruch said. That includes a “substantial” expansion of transformer and switchgear capacity in North America, where a manufacturing hub under construction in North Carolina is already sold out for its first two years of operation, Ferraro said.

The growth of the installed gas fleet will also drive long-term maintenance needs: Siemens Energy expects revenue from gas turbine services to more than double by 2035. Twenty-year service contracts signed this year carry margins five percentage points higher than in the past, Ferraro said, thanks to increased market prices and decreased costs.

The company's Gas Services division is focused on a vertical integration strategy that has the company buying upstream suppliers to drive efficiency, Bruch said.

To further strengthen its focus on the utility sector, Siemens Energy plans to spin out its Transformation of Industry division, which serves industrial customers, as an independent company. Siemens is seeking a co-investor to help finance the launch of the new company, which Siemens plans to carve out after the parent company finishes its transition to the new Omterra brand name.

A company press release pitched the spinoff as necessary to avoid limiting what the Transformation of Industry division could achieve because the division competes for business in sectors — including, but not limited to, data centers — that move far faster than the utility sector.

#5706. Solar lease holdouts still see value in privately-owned residential projects

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects. The ITC is a historic renewable energy subsidy that provides a 30% tax credit against the total cost of an eligible project, and it is currently available to the commercial and utility-scale solar segments.

A residential solar project in New York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions. Credit: Nickels Energy Solutions

After 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned. However, a loophole in the tax credit language has allowed leased or “third party-owned” (TPO) solar projects to still receive the ITC (25D) on residential solar projects. In this scenario, it matters who owns the solar project, not necessarily where it’s built. The project can be subsidized because it is owned by a commercial company, and not the homeowner.

Some residential solar installers are still strictly pursuing and installing privately-owned solar projects. Nickels Energy Solutions (NES), a residential solar contractor working in Central New York believes a privately-owned PV system is still the better deal for the customer.

“We don’t have the same offers as some of the bigger companies,” said Kevin Nickels, VP of sales with NES. “If you can offer leases, it’s like the ‘haves and have-nots.’ I don’t have that loophole or that trick up my sleeve, so it forces me to get the project sold, while I’m as sharp as I can be with margins to make it somewhat competitive.”

TPO solar transactions are typically arranged at a lower up-front cost than a wholly owned solar project. Lease contract lengths vary by provider, and financiers have surety in these transactions because the projects will be built with products from an approved vendor list (AVL). Products on an AVL can qualify for a domestic content subsidy, another tax credit in addition to the ITC, because they are manufactured using a certain percentage of domestic components.

These are premium products vetted for AVLs. But it can also mean that installers are paying premium prices for components in building TPO solar projects.

Nickels believes that, while a privately owned residential solar project will cost more at the start, the combination of expensive components and interest rates for financing over a lease term — with factors like rate increases — can cost a customer more in the long run.

“I don’t think all leases are bad,” he said. “I just don’t think it’s what’s best for the industry or the homeowner.”

Rudy Wright, owner of Wright-Way Solar of Tyler, Texas, has shifted the company’s focus from building new projects to servicing existing systems. As the ITC exited the residential solar market, so did many of the lenders financing these projects. Without lending options, Wright-Way’s installation output has slowed down, and those clients who can afford solar are paying with cash or using a home equity loan to cover the cost.

Despite that, Wright said he isn’t very interested in building leased solar projects.

Wright-Way Solar built a solar plus storage project at a Ranch in Texas featuring arrays that are facing east, west and south. Credit: Wright-Way Solar

“I do think it cost me some of those entry level clients, but every time I analyzed the financing end of it, I felt like I was benefitting my company and the industry more than the customer,” Wright said. “I haven’t seen the angle where bringing a pre-purchase agreement or bringing a lease agreement has enough ironclad return for the customer.”

Tyler is a unique market for solar because many of Wright-Way’s customers are trying to make their properties more resilient, and less reliant on the grid, by installing solar and storage, and not just seeking cost savings for their energy use. Wright has installed solar plus storage systems on Texan ranches at a scale close a small commercial project.

That promise of resilience is still enough reason for some people to commission a solar project in Texas, where the state’s independent electrical grid operator has faltered and experienced dangerous outages in recent years.

“Folks realize money in the bank doesn’t do you any good if the power goes out,” Wright said.

NES is still building a steady pipeline of residential solar projects in New York. Nickels said that has been possible in part because many of its clients are upper-middle class; but New York also maintains an incentive program for solar projects, NY-Sun, which includes a 25% state tax credit for residential systems.

“The OBBBA caught a lot of states flat-footed,” Nickels said. “Without federal support, it puts a lot of pressure on what the state is offering.”

Some states’ solar subsidy programs have stepped in where federal support has diminished since the OBBBA was passed. The North Carolina Clean Energy Technology Center maintains the Database of State Incentives for Renewables & Efficiency, which analyzes which states currently have policies and incentives supporting clean energy developments. Every state has policy enabling solar projects, but not necessarily cost incentives for individual projects.

While traditional residential solar projects have lost a significant subsidy, the reality is that energy costs have risen in response to new grid demands from hyperscale data centers and oil scarcity from the United States’ war in Iran. Sure, a privately owned residential solar project won’t receive the ITC, but it can still stabilize energy costs without them.

“We lost a big incentive, but the rate increase is proportional,” Nickels said.

Billy Ludt is managing editor of Solar Power World and currently covers topics on mounting, inverters, installation and operations.

#5704. Cummins Told Electrolyser Customers to Stop. Who Keeps the Hydrogen Plants Running?

Cummins is withdrawing from new electrolyser sales, but its customers have a problem that cannot be handled by closing a sales office. In September, its Hydrogenics subsidiaries recommended that customers stop using HyLYZER electrolysers following a review of operating data. The company disclosed the recommendation in its November quarterly report, said that it had not launched a recall, and was still assessing what modifications might be needed for equipment to return to service. It had not established the cost of resolving the issue and warned that the eventual financial effect could be material.

Cummins had a substantial position in the PEM electrolyser business. Accelera reports more than 45 HyLYZER 500 systems and more than 20 HyLYZER 1000 systems rated at 5 MW each. Using those minimum reported system counts and equipment ratings, its historical deployments represent roughly 145–213 MW, equivalent to 11–16% of the IEA’s projected 1.3 GW global PEM installed base at the end of 2026. Cummins has not published the number of HyLYZER plants covered by its September recommendation. The company is leaving a sizeable equipment estate requiring expert maintenance, field engineers and potential safety modifications.

The timing makes the situation consequential. Cummins announced in February that it intended to cease new commercial electrolyser activity, while continuing existing customer commitments. Its 2025 Accelera restructuring and impairment charges reached $458 million across several actions, including the electrolyser retreat. It is reducing specialist capacity at the same time as installed equipment needs engineering attention. Revenue from new orders can disappear faster than warranties, service obligations and safety responsibilities.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing on Cummins’ hydrogen hangover examines the HyLYZER warning, the customer projects and the financial implications of manufacturers leaving shrinking markets. The underlying evidence and project comparisons are in the full analysis.

The problem now moves from selling hardware to keeping it safe and serviceable. Investigating field data, testing modifications, certifying repair procedures and maintaining proprietary controls requires specialist teams. Those teams must remain capable long after the sales pipeline and the business unit built around it have contracted.

Estonia’s Stargate Hydrogen has taken over Cummins’ legacy HySTAT alkaline electrolyser platform and supplies replacement stacks and service for a fleet of more than 400 installations. That handover shows how intellectual property, manufacturing capability and field-service expertise can survive an OEM exit. Cummins’ HyLYZER PEM fleet needs its own engineering and aftermarket solution.

For owners, the financial question also depends on the purpose of the hydrogen. Air Liquide’s 20 MW Bécancour installation and Linde’s 35 MW Niagara Falls project serve companies with industrial hydrogen customers and alternative supply networks. Interruptions can mean lost sales, replacement purchases and costs of maintaining customer commitments. An owner with contracted industrial demand has a commercial reason to restore production, provided the equipment can meet the required safety standards and the replacement supply costs justify it.

Florida Power & Light’s Cavendish project presents another decision. Its 25 MW HyLYZER installation converts electricity to hydrogen for limited blending into natural gas used in power generation. Even without a stop-use issue, that application has to compete with using electricity directly or obtaining reliable grid services by other means. At an illustrative 55 kWh/kg of electrolyser electricity and 60% combined-cycle generation efficiency, about 36% of the original electricity returns after converting it to hydrogen and burning it, before compression and storage. Input power at $50/MWh would cost roughly $138/MWh of recovered electricity before equipment and operating expenses. Repairing the electrolyser would not change that conversion arithmetic.

The economic difference appears again at Hysolar’s Nieuwegein installation. A 2025 KWR H-Flex evaluation documented project delays, higher costs and hydrogen demand expanding more slowly than planned. Its electrolyser, dedicated pipeline, refuelling station and vehicle customers are linked by a common demand forecast. Better equipment performance helps only when enough customers will buy the hydrogen at prices covering production and delivery. The same distinction applies to demonstration projects combining buses, heating, electricity and gas blending: several proposed uses do not guarantee several profitable markets.

Manufacturers face the cost of retaining the people and intellectual property to support complex equipment long after the expected growth market has contracted. Cummins’ separate exit from its low-pressure fuel-cell business illustrates the potential bill: in March 2026, it made a $175 million net payment as part of a sale, cancellation of commitments and claims settlement, producing a $199 million accounting charge. Those are fuel-cell transaction figures, not estimated HyLYZER repair costs. The PEM matter remains unquantified.

The customers’ cost can exceed the repair bill. Owners need a safe restart route, long-term supply of stacks and controls, a price for replacement hydrogen during outages, and buyers able to pay for the output afterward. Lenders face a thinner resale market for specialised plants when their OEM leaves. Public funders face grant, regulated cost-recovery and guarantee liabilities when projects stop operating.

The wider hydrogen market makes these questions urgent. The IEA’s Global Hydrogen Review 2026 finds that global demand still sits overwhelmingly in traditional industry and refining. Only about one-fifth of newly signed low-emissions hydrogen offtake volumes in 2025 had firm contractual commitments. A producer, refuelling-station operator and vehicle buyer can each invest on the assumption that the other two will grow. That is one demand risk distributed across three balance sheets, not three independent investments.

The next investment decision needs a safe route back to service, contracted customers, dependable parts supply and a costed exit alternative. Governments should direct support toward industrial customers who need hydrogen and can pay for it, rather than finance energy-carrier applications that lose to direct electricity. Cummins is exposing the long tail of earlier commitments. Other suppliers, buyers and lenders still control their next decisions.

The complete Cummins analysis compares industrial-gas plants, fuel-substitution pilots, refuelling systems and legacy equipment obligations. The earlier Cummins–Alstom assessment shows how similar service liabilities can persist in fuel-cell transportation.

#5703. Grid operators file closely watched large load interconnection reforms at FERC

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The PJM Interconnection proposed revamping its interconnection process by studying large load and generation interconnection requests in a single, one-year review.

Most major U.S. grid operators have now submitted their highly anticipated proposals for interconnecting data centers and other large loads to the grid in response to directives issued by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

FERC in June issued “show cause” orders saying that it appeared that regional transmission organizations and others lacked adequate rules for adding large loads to the grid. FERC asked them to propose reforms to address the agency’s concerns or to explain why their existing rules were just and reasonable.

FERC detailed five issues it wanted the grid operators to address in their large load interconnection rules: efficient transmission service application and study processes, including the consideration of alternative transmission technologies; prevention of cost shifts and transparency into transmission costs; co-location and behind-the-meter generation; new transmission services for flexible large loads; and a study process for generating facilities that serve “electrically proximate” large loads and co-located loads.

The move by FERC comes amid a surge in data center development in many U.S. regions and a corresponding pushback on that development, which includes concerns that existing utility customers will pay for some of the data center-related electric infrastructure.

Below is a summary of the proposals at FERC, which were filed on Monday, except for ISO New England’s. The Southwest Power Pool is slated to file its proposal by Friday.

The centerpiece of PJM’s plan is a Fast Energization Process, under which the grid operator would revamp its interconnection study process by studying large load and generation interconnection requests in a single, one-year process — about twice as fast as the current process, according to PJM.

In its filing on Monday, PJM said its proposed Fast Energization Process is designed to address “insufficiently fast interconnection processes for load and generation, parallel and duplicative study processes, speculative requests, limited visibility into the drivers of transmission upgrades, and an ongoing resource adequacy shortfall.”

The proposed process marks “the next evolution of PJM’s interconnection process and further enhancement to the currently effective Cycle process,” Donald Bielak, director of interconnection planning at PJM, told FERC in a separate filing.

PJM’s overall proposal also addresses co-location and behind-the-meter generation rules that were at issue in a separate show cause proceeding, according to the grid operator. PJM filed a separate proposal that requires large computational loads to be able to ride through grid disturbances.

PJM’s transmission owners filed their own proposed tariffs that establish rates, cost allocation, cost recovery mechanisms, financial protections, revenue-crediting requirements and transparency measures for transmission service they provide to co-located loads and large loads.

“The proposed reforms strengthen accountability and protect existing customers,” CAISO told FERC. “They improve transparency, operational visibility, technical standards, cost responsibility, and protection against speculative development.”

The CAISO and transmission owner tariff revisions create streamlined paths for large loads to connect to the electric system, according to the grid operator. “Standardized application information, deposits, milestones, study coordination, and service agreements will make the process more transparent and predictable,” CAISO said.

As part of its proposal, CAISO plans to offer new service options for flexible large loads that can cut their electric use when transmission capability is unavailable.

In its filing on Friday, ISO-NE and the region’s transmission owners said they fully addressed FERC’s show cause order. In response to the agency’s transparency concerns, ISO-NE proposed that it maintain on its website a list of the network upgrades identified for each large load, categorized by upgrade type, and the cost estimates for those upgrades.

To address FERC’s concerns about resource adequacy in New England, ISO-NE said it plans to require that large loads bring their own new capacity and that certain large loads will be excluded from ISO-NE’s capacity market’s installed capacity requirement. The grid operator plans to work with stakeholders to craft the details of its proposed framework, with a goal of filing a proposal at FERC later this year.

MISO said its proposal builds on its other reform plans recently filed at FERC: the Zero Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement, Interconnection Reliability Requirements for Large Loads and Large Load Addition Resource Study.

The just-filed proposal includes a Large Load Project Review process, new transmission service options and tariff revisions and pro forma cost recovery agreements designed to prevent cost shifting onto existing utility customers, MISO said. In a separate filing Monday, MISO proposed Grid Responsive Integration Transmission Service for large loads that can limit their electric use under certain price and reliability conditions.

MISO’s proposals at FERC represent “an important milestone, not an endpoint,” the grid operator said. “MISO remains committed to further enhancing its planning, operational, and market frameworks as experience is gained and system needs grow.”

Among other things, NYISO’s proposal provides new types of transmission services — Firm Withdrawal Service and Non-Firm Withdrawal Service — that reflect the unique characteristics of NYISO’s transmission model and of co-located large loads, large load with behind-the-meter generation, and flexible large loads, the grid operator said.

The proposal includes a compromise approach to resource adequacy requirements, called the State Exempt Load Project exception, which aims to reconcile the NYISO’s reliability responsibilities with the New York Public Service Commission resource adequacy authority, the grid operator said.

The PSC has launched a proceeding to address state-jurisdictional interconnection reforms that will likely influence the evolution of NYISO’s large load rules, the grid operator noted. New York transmission owners also filed a complementary large load proposal at FERC.
