#5653. Are There Any V12 Engines That Could Be Called 'Dependable?'

A V12 engine under the bonnet is a symbol of automotive decadence, telling the world that you've made it and who cares about fuel consumption. Sure, there are plenty of engines that deliver as much performance, but few that exude extravagance and luxury in quite the same way. Still, can V12s be dependable? You might assume not, given their specialized nature and low-volume production.

V12s are installed in high-end sedans and limousines, in mid-engined supercars, and in a handful of opulent SUVs and 4x4s. But they're not that numerous in the grand scheme of production vehicles.

One of the first uses of the V12 came in 1913, when, in the UK, Louis Coatalen, the chief engineer of Sunbeam Motor Car Company, stuffed a new type of aircraft engine called the Mohawk into one of the company's race cars. Subsequently, "Toodles V" was born: a machine which, after a few hiccups, went on to set eight world speed-over-distance records at Brooklands racetrack.

After Toodles and before WWII, V12s grew in popularity for their smoothness and power, with the North American auto industry providing the bulk of them, even during the Great Depression of 1929: think Packard Twin Six, the Auburn 12, the Cadillac V-12, and the Lincoln series K.

But when Lincoln ceased production of the V12 in 1948, that was that for American V12s. No car company has made one in the U.S. since, and production was mainly left to Europe. Ferrari made its legendary "Colombo" V12, Lamborghini's 1963 V12 would eventually underpin the gorgeous Miura, and even Jaguar brought a 5.3-liter V12 engine to the E-Type in 1971.

There are still a few V12s in production today that you can buy with a new-car warranty, which are likely reliable, but what about those of yesteryear? Here's a look at the most dependable.

If you're after a V12 that's about as widespread and dependable as can be, then the Mercedes M120 is the one to seek out. Mercedes had been working on the idea of a passenger car with a V12 since the 1950s (and considered putting one in its 600 Pullman limo), but it was beaten to the punch by BMW's adoption of the 5.0-liter V12 in 1987's E32 750i. Mercedes didn't get its M120 V12 to market until 1991 in the W140-series S-Class. The 600 badge was given to the W140-series S-Class, the related CL coupe, and the R129 Mercedes SL due to the engine's displacement.

The M120 was a considerably more advanced engine than BMW's V12. It featured an aluminum-alloy block, a forged crankshaft, and LH-Jetronic fuel injection, along with dual throttle bodies, mass airflow sensors, and ECUs. Producing 402 horsepower and 428 pounds-feet of torque, the M120 had enough grunt to push the heavy 600 SE and SEL models from 0 to 60 mph in around six seconds.

What makes the M120 so desirable today, though, is its dependability. There are a few known weak points, such as oil leaks around the valve covers, the front timing covers, the lower oil pan, and the front crank seal, along with worn engine mounts. But aside from these relatively minor issues, this V12 is known for its reliability and solidity. Furthermore, owners of such high-end Mercs are likely to have kept up with their maintenance.

One final seal of approval comes in the form of the M120's subsequent use in the middle of the Pagani Zonda, a supercar classic we'll always love: a 7.3-liter development of the V12 powered various iterations, culminating in a near-800-hp final edition.

Japan is a country that has not wholeheartedly embraced the V12 engine. In fact, it has made but one road-going engine of this configuration in history, although it turns out to be one of the most reliable V12s you could imagine. It's called the 1GZ-FE, a naturally aspirated 5.0-liter lump with variable valve timing, two ECUs, and enough redundancy built in that it can run on one bank of six cylinders if necessary. The engine powered the second-generation Toyota Century.

A big plus point of the 1GZ is that it's not what you'd call a stressed V12. In its original 1997 incarnation for the Century model, the Japanese "gentleman's agreement" put in place to prevent a horsepower war meant that Toyota claimed a peak power output of just 276 horsepower, with torque rated at up to 355 pounds-feet. It was never going to be one of the most powerful JDM engines ever made, even if its horsepower was higher than the domestic advertising suggested.

If that's not a big enough perk, know that like so many Toyota engines, the 1GZ-FE would accommodate a heck of a lot of tuning. In fact, the notorious Smokey Nagata – founder of Top Secret and the man who pushed a Supra to 194 mph on a British motorway in 1998 – later built another Supra with a Century's V12 in it. Only that was adorned with a pair of HKS GT2540 turbos, liberating 930 hp and a top speed of over 220 mph.

When the engine was launched, Toyota published an engineering paper stating, amongst other things, that the 1GZ-FE was more reliable than its competitors, and though the sample size is small, it has been proven to be a dependable V12, with nothing other than age-related failures of minor parts generally reported.

The original BMW V12, the M70, started an entire line of engines that went into the 7 Series as well as the 8 Series. BMW's M70 successor, the M73, was employed by Rolls-Royce starting in 1998 with the Silver Seraph. Rolls began using a V12 in its Phantom III (1936-1939), but after trying that 7.3-liter monster out for size, it eventually dedicated itself to inline-6 and V8 engines. Rolls-Royce did not use a V12 again until the 1998 Silver Seraph.

Perhaps the most famous application of a BMW V12 was the S70/2, designed by Paul Rosche, which was the incredible engine that powered the legendary McLaren F1 with 627 horsepower. Though maintenance costs are high, the engine itself is robust.

Both Ferrari and Lamborghini's V12s are highly tuned, and of course, they're installed in the sorts of cars that command huge fees on the used market. Nonetheless, the 5.5-liter engine in the Ferrari 456 GT, for example, is supposed to be fairly dependable, as long as it is subjected to regular (and expensive) maintenance.

Aston Martin has been making production V12s since the DB7 Vantage of 1999, and while these "AML" units were not just two Ford Duratec V6s welded together, there was plenty of Ford-derived DNA in the British engine courtesy of Ford's advanced powertrain division. It's generally dependable, so long as owners keep up with maintenance. Oil starvation to the crankshaft is one of the more common issues.

Finally, Jaguar had a good array of V12s in such cars as the E-Type and XJ models. While the mechanicals are reasonably durable, these engines are frequently let down by their electrics.

#5652. China’s Electric Heavy Trucks Are Taking Sales from Diesel and LNG

In September 2026, battery-electric trucks captured 49.8% of China’s new domestic heavy-truck registrations. Of 65,800 trucks registered, 32,800 ran on batteries. Another 36 used hydrogen fuel cells. Battery electric accounted for more than 99% of the broader new-energy category. China’s freight operators are buying batteries at a scale that puts diesel and LNG suppliers under pressure.

The shift has gathered speed. Battery electric accounted for about 13% of domestic heavy-truck registrations in 2024, 28% in 2025 and nearly 38% in the first nine months of 2026. The figures come from compulsory-insurance registrations for trucks sold into the domestic market, excluding exports. China’s total domestic truck market remains below its pre-pandemic levels. Battery trucks are gaining share while the market for new heavy trucks remains constrained.

From May through September, new-energy heavy trucks exceeded 40% of new registrations for five straight months. The category reached approximately 226,400 vehicles in the first nine months, up 64% from the same period in 2025, and nearly 99% were battery electric. Tractor units that pull semi-trailers are leading the change. In September, 64.48% of new domestic tractor registrations belonged to the new-energy category. Electric trucks are moving freight on ordinary commercial routes, including work beyond ports and industrial yards.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing traces China’s heavy-truck sales from 2015 through 2026, examines real freight costs and charging choices, and assesses the consequences for manufacturers, logistics companies and fuel demand.

The operating economics explain much of the appeal. Trucks earn money by carrying cargo, so annual kilometres, payload, electricity prices, charging stops and vehicle availability matter as much as the price on the invoice. High-mileage routes make electricity and maintenance savings more valuable. A costly grid connection or charging queue can eat into those savings. Fleet operators need to evaluate the truck and its route together.

Recent ICCT case studies document how those economics play out. A Guangdong warehouse fleet of 28 electric trucks had estimated five-year ownership costs 16% below comparable diesel trucks. In Yangtze River Delta express delivery, 50 electric tractor-trailers working routes of 300–500 km achieved a narrower 3% advantage over six years without purchase incentives. Another operation covering 900 km a day with strategically placed high-power charging showed estimated ownership costs 19% below diesel. The differences reflect route, utilization and charging arrangements.

Those three operations offer a more useful procurement lesson than a single quoted range figure. The operator starts with cargo, schedules and energy access, then selects equipment. The narrow 3% margin in express delivery also shows why financing and charging costs can determine whether a viable electric route makes money.

Battery swapping has carved out a sizable part of this market. In September, 20.09% of newly registered battery-electric heavy trucks were classified as swap-capable. That compares with 22.92% across January–September 2026 and 30.39% for all of 2025. The number of swap-classified trucks continued to rise, while conventional charging gained a larger share of the expanding electric market. China’s registration classification also includes some trucks with leased batteries that are recharged rather than exchanged.

Swapping fits dense, repeatable freight operations such as steelworks, ports and bulk-material haulage. Fleet operators and station owners can standardize vehicles and use stations often enough to pay for batteries held in inventory. Conventional charging serves a wider range of routes and can fit scheduled stops, overnight parking and depot operations. Both approaches depend on predictable truck traffic and reliable electricity connections.

China is building infrastructure around those freight patterns. Yunnan commissioned 3,350 km of heavy-truck charging corridors in 2025, with 113 stations and 869 connectors. Fujian opened a 649 km coastal corridor in October 2026, including 15 charging stations and eight swapping stations. The IEA’s 2026 charging review describes the concentration of heavy-vehicle charging around freight corridors and industrial centres. Long-haul coverage still has gaps, but the network is expanding where trucks already have work to do.

Hydrogen has found little traction alongside this expansion. China registered 689 fuel-cell heavy trucks in the first nine months of 2026, compared with more than 223,000 battery-electric trucks. LNG has a much larger installed customer base, although its advantage over diesel has narrowed as gas prices change. Battery trucks offer a different cost structure built around drivetrain efficiency and lower maintenance needs. That makes the competition increasingly difficult for equipment and fuel suppliers dependent on combustion engines.

Sales changes take years to work through the operating fleet. Kpler projects that new-energy trucks, predominantly battery electric, will account for about 8% of Chinese heavy trucks in service at the end of 2026. It also estimates they will displace about 230,000 barrels of diesel per day compared with moving the same freight using diesel trucks. Freight vehicles with high daily utilization can have a large effect on fuel demand before they become a majority of vehicles on the road.

China’s June 2026 heavy-truck programme joins purchasing incentives, grid access, charging corridors, financing and logistics planning. Its 2030 targets include a 40% share of new-energy heavy-truck sales, a 20% share of the operating fleet and 30,000 km of zero-carbon freight corridors. Monthly new sales have already surpassed the sales-share target. Building and replacing enough vehicles to reach the fleet target will take longer.

Other countries have different electricity tariffs, road networks and freight routes, but the procurement method travels. Start with the actual jobs trucks perform. Identify routes with strong electric economics, plan the charging and grid connections those routes require, and finance vehicles and infrastructure as one programme. Other drivetrains can compete where their operating costs or performance are better. The evidence from China’s largest commercial freight applications increasingly favours batteries.

The complete TFIE Strategy Briefing includes the historical registration series, the ICCT ownership-cost cases, charging and swapping corridors, and fleet-turnover analysis. TFIE Strategy works with fleets, utilities and policymakers on freight-electrification scenarios and investment decisions.

#5651. 'He Should Talk to His Primary Care Doctor About That'

— We should treat the patient in front of us whenever possible

One spring day during my neurology rotation, a man in his nineties came to our clinic. He was walking with a cane but otherwise remarkably independent, with the air of distinguished gentlemanliness a brown tweed jacket lends. We had an instant connection. Talking for just a few moments, we realized he hailed from my own family's ancestral town. As I spoke with him in his native language, he soon began calling me "pota" for "grandson." Quickly though, my resident and I also realized our patient was with us by mistake. Perhaps due to a miscommunication, or an administrative error, he thought he was at his primary care physician (PCP). He had been experiencing constipation.

After we clarified the confusion, my resident -- someone who taught me a great deal -- asked me to walk our patient out to the front desk and help him schedule a primary care appointment. The front desk said the next PCP appointment wouldn't be available for 7 weeks. I went to ask the resident if we could do something to help our patient; after all, while constipation may turn out to be a complex symptom either due to a serious condition (colorectal cancer, sigmoid volvulus) or as a precursor to downstream pathology (diverticulosis, fecal impaction), it is also quite common among older adults.

Both the resident and I had rotated on internal medicine and knew the questions to ask to identify any red flags and suggest a bowel regimen. And we had the time -- our patient didn't have a neurological concern, but he still had the appointment slot. Yet, when I returned to the clinic room to ask my resident if we could give our patient the relevant advice, he looked up from the queue of notes he was finishing and replied: "He should talk to his PCP about that."

Economics tell us that workforce efficiency is maximized when everyone spends time on what they are uniquely best at doing: labor arbitrage. As a management consultant prior to medical school, I spent years evangelizing this concept of "top of license work" to clients -- mostly large academic and nonprofit hospital systems. And I still believe in the principle broadly, albeit with perhaps a bit more reticence and understanding more nuance than before.

Top-of-license work in medicine doesn't only apply vertically across levels of training; it also operates horizontally, across fields. Patient outcomes are generally maximized when neurologists focus on diseases of the nervous system and gastroenterologists the digestive system because each specialty is doing work only they can do. Yet, that day in the neurology clinic taught me a nuance to this perspective.

At the end of the day, all physicians should consider themselves doctors first, and specialists second. Medical specialization shouldn't absolve specialists of the duty to help the patient before them -- especially when doing so requires minimal time and resources -- even if the patient's concern is not directly within their field.

Of course, there are challenges to this perspective. I can empathize with the medico-legal concerns of a neurologist who is served a subpoena and deposed by a lawyer: "Firstly, why did you manage this constipation? And why did you not order XYZ tests for this patient with constipation who turned out to have colorectal cancer?" And I recognize the confusion medical teams may feel when checking charts and seeing who prescribed certain medications: "Why is the prescribing doctor for this patient's cetirizine (Zyrtec) an orthopedic surgeon?"

These concerns are real. But primary care is a limited resource too. The dumping of basic tasks on primary care -- a field with its own specialized expertise that is often not recognized -- has been discussed ad nauseam; specialists should help relieve this burden when possible.

Labor arbitrage and top of license work still apply when specialists help patients with "primary care problems." However, because of the design of our healthcare system, there is little structural incentive for physicians to work outside of their typical scopes. If, for instance, we financially incentivized all of a patient's physicians by the same quality metrics, specialists would be incentivized not just in their field, but across the spectrum of the patient's health. Or even if we had less insurance churn, payers would perhaps better leverage incentives within their networks to promote overall health.

Responding to incentives does not mean physicians have moral failings. It shows they are human. But if we continue to depend on our system as currently designed, we will continue to have rampant "moral alibis" -- a term coined by Sachin Jain, MD, MBA, to highlight how physicians at times emphasize problems with the system to escape responsibility for personal decisions -- that limit the impact of our care.

The vast majority of physicians enter medicine to help patients. It is the design of our system that has forced practice to occur in unnatural ways. But perhaps while we solve these structural problems, we can start changing things by treating the patient in front of us -- one case of constipation at a time.

#5650. The Rising Tide Of Distributed Energy Resources

Centralized power plants can trip widespread brownouts or blackouts when under stress. They make fat targets for enemy weapons, too. In contrast, distributed energy resources (DERs for short) can improve overall resiliency in the face of both natural and human-made disasters, while also enabling ratepayers to take advantage of utility discounts, and even earn revenue from their personal energy assets. The DERs field includes — but is not limited to — rooftop solar, EV charging stations, and home batteries. And, we ain’t seen nothing yet. DERs stakeholders have also begun moving into the distributed computing field as well.

DERs first surfaced on the CleanTechnica radar in the early 2000’s during the Obama administration, when the US Department of Energy began promoting decentralized, home-and community-based energy resources as the leading characteristic of a modernized and more resilient electricity grid. Made possible by the falling cost of solar, wind, and energy storage, the agency’s embrace of small-scale, localized electricity generation was a sharp contrast with the traditional emphasis on large centralized power plants for energy security (see more DERs background here).

Nowadays the DERs field embraces practically any non-centralized power generation resource, regardless of size or type. The DERs field can include, for example, a new gas power plant commissioned to run an adjacent AI data center.

To get some perspective on the journey of DERs since the early 2000’s, consider the case of the leading rooftop solar installer Sunrun. After launching in 2007, Sunrun segued into energy storage and virtual power plants, with “virtual” referring to smart grid technology that coordinates thousands of far-flung energy producing (and consuming) devices to balance supply and demand at peak periods of consumption.

For the record, Sunrun now presents itself as a storage-first company. The company’s focus remains on renewable energy but the storage field is source-agnostic, embracing practically every energy resource on the planet.

Sunrun CEO Mary Powell also prefers to use “distributed” instead of “virtual” in reference to decentralized power systems, to emphasize that hardware is the foundational element. As of this month, Sunrun ranks as the biggest distributed power plant in the US, with solar and storage assets spread among 164,000 enrolled households.

Back in 2021, Sunrun entered into an installation partnership with the home energy management startup SPAN, known for its next-generation home electrical panels among other products, and that layed the ground work for a partnership on distributed computing systems. Earlier this year, SPAN introduced XFRA, a new product consisting of computer nodes to be staged at homes and smaller commercial spaces to form a distributed data center. The model is similar in concept to the familiar Internet-enabled citizen scientist platform, except that XFRA deploys its own nodes instead of using a participant’s personal computer.

This past September, Sunrun announced its selection as an authorized installation partner for XFRA with a focus on new home developments, aiming for gigawatt-scale distributed computing networks beginning in Texas and other selected markets. “Sunrun’s battery-plus-solar systems will maintain reliable electricity for both the homes and the XFRA compute nodes, while preventing the overloading of local distribution infrastructure—allowing SPAN to maximize node deployment.,” Sunrun explains.

“By pairing home energy generation and storage with XFRA compute nodes, we are unlocking new economic value for our customers and for Sunrun, while also solving certain speed-to-power constraints that would otherwise limit AI deployment,” Sunrun CEO Mary Powell elaborated in a press statement.

Arch Rao, founder and CEO of SPAN, also chipped in his two cents. “We can now drastically increase our penetration of XFRA compute nodes by pairing them with Sunrun energy systems to deliver cost-effective AI compute capacity at unprecedented speed while also reducing compute cost for certain AI applications,” Rao said.

Back when the Energy Department initially began promoting DERs as a function of the energy transition, the agency used the term “prosumer” to describe ratepayers who are empowered to engage with their local power grid as a renewable energy producer, not simply as a passive consumer. The distributed data center adds another layer of engagement to the prosumer mix.

At a personal appearance during Climate Week in New York City in September, Powell referenced distributed computing as the latest demonstration of the company’s ongoing dialog with its customers and other stakeholders, leading to innovative new products that put more power management tools in the hands of ratepayers.

Powell reiterated the point during an appearance at the 2026 “DERVOS” summit at the Brooklyn Navy Yard on November 5, and the DERVOS gathering itself provides further insights into the widening scope of DERs activity.

“DERVOS” is a play on Davos, which is shorthand for the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum. Like the World Economic Forum, DERs stakeholders have emerged in force upon the global economy as well as here in the US, stretching far from its do-it-yourself roots in the off-gridder movement of the 1970’s.

The event itself is the brainchild of the collaborative trade organization DER Task Force. The group formally launched in 2019 but it claims roots much earlier, in the 1970’s-era New York City activist organization Energy Task Force, whose activities were highlighted by the installation of a wind turbine in the city — illegally, of course.

By the time DERVOS 2026 rolled around, the DER Task Force had become an organization with a reach far beyond New York, and it has also embraced the size-doesn’t-matter ethos  under the slogan, “Everything is DER.”

“That’s what we mean by Everything is DER: not that everything is small, or even literally ‘distributed,’ but that the center of gravity is shifting toward energy resources that are closer to load and controlled by those who need the power,” the Task Force explains (emphasis theirs).

“Sometimes that shift is bottoms-up, sometimes it’s centrally planned, but either way, DERs aren’t the sideshow anymore. They’re the main event,” they add.

I’ll have much more to report from DERVOS 2026 in the coming days and weeks, but for the time being let’s go back to the foundational idea of improving grid resiliency and security. Climate change aside, in recent years Russia and the US have both provided textbook cases for transitioning out of energy systems that involve building fat, juicy infrastructure targets for attack, alongside precariously long energy transportation systems. If you have any thoughts about that, drop a note in the comment thread.

Image: The renewable energy “prosumer” envisioned by the US Department of Energy in the early 2000’s has become the sophisticated distributed energy resources manager of today (graphic by Sara Harman courtesy of US DOE).

Tina has been covering advanced energy technology, military sustainability, emerging materials, biofuels, ESG and related policy and political matters for CleanTechnica since 2009. Follow her @tinamcasey on LinkedIn, Mastodon or Bluesky.

#5649. Slate Sells 'Screenless GPS' For Its Trucks, Which Is Just A Map

Slate, maker of the barebones $26,400 electric truck that I desperately want to see succeed despite my worries about its competition, is all about simplicity. Simple truck, simple purchase price, simple construction, simple accessories. So what happens when buyers want something more complex — something like GPS, which requires satellite connections, maps, screens, and code? Well, the company does it the old fashioned way by stamping its brand on a Rand McNally Road Atlas and selling it as "Screenless GPS."

The automaker is selling these atlases for $30, and on the website it's currently marked as sold out. The product description reads, "This is the original navigation system — no signal required. Spiral bound, large print, and ready for wherever your Slate takes you. Covers the US, Canada, and Mexico. Limited edition." This particular book is the 2027 Rand McNally EasyFinder Road Atlas, and it includes "7 curated Rand McNally road trips."

Rand McNally, for the younger readers out there, makes books of maps that it calls its road atlases. I grew up with a road atlas wedged between the driver's seat and center console of my mom's car, and I certainly remember thumbing through its pages while bored — behavior my mom encouraged, so I'd know how to read a map by the time I started driving myself. It's certainly a skill the average Slate buyer has, and maybe the folks that appreciate a simple truck will likewise appreciate a simple way to navigate it around.

Paper maps have had a bit of a renaissance as we all get ever more tired of our constantly-increasing screentime. Backcountry Discovery Routes has worked with Butler Maps for years to create paper maps of its BDR routes for those looking to go screenless on the trails, and it seems Slate is hoping to bring the same enthusiasm to road maps with its Rand McNally tie-in. I'm just hoping the promotion Slate is doing for its map, like the Instagram post above, is all tongue in cheek. If the company really means "analog pinch to zoom" is a feature, it comes off a bit I HATE WIFE AND PHOEN.

For most of us, a phone mount suction-cupped to the windshield will make a better navigation solution than a Rand McNally shoved next to the center console. For Slate's target market, buyers who actively miss simpler, older cars and want a return to that kind of design, the bent and worn pages of a worn Road Atlas may provide a bit of the nostalgia they're looking for in an all-electric truck. After all, they probably had one in their old Ranger all those years ago.

#5648. Chemicals in Many Everyday Items Pose a Growing Threat, U.N. Report Says

— Health-related costs from exposure is estimated to exceed $1.1 trillion annually worldwide

Chemicals in many everyday items that tinker with a body's hormones are a growing threat to human health and the environment, and science now better understands the harm they cause, a new United Nations report said Tuesday.

Endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) are found in many plastic items, personal care products, pharmaceuticals, toys, household goods, electronics, and pesticides. The new report, written by scientists, estimates the health-related costs from exposure to these chemicals exceed $1.1 trillion annually worldwide. It calls for urgent, coordinated international action to protect human health and the environment.

The policies and regulations to transform the products and sectors causing widespread exposure to these chemicals remain "fragmented and insufficient," it says.

The U.N. Environment Program (UNEP) and World Health Organization issued the report.

"This report is an important step towards a safer world, free from exposure to EDCs," the two U.N. bodies wrote in the foreword. "Solutions do exist. Some safer alternatives are available. The task for policymakers is to ensure that these solutions and alternatives are deployed -- to protect human, animal and planetary health, and save trillions of dollars each year."

The "state of the science" report describes what scientists have learned about exposure to EDCs and their effects since 2012. Previous reports assessed the science on EDCs in 2002 and 2012 to inform policymakers and guide action.

Jacqueline Alvarez, PhD, chief of the UNEP Chemicals and Health Branch, said the new report builds on those assessments, while reflecting a field that has advanced substantially in the breadth of health effects documented, in the sophistication of exposure science, in the development of testing and assessment methodologies, and in a growing understanding of the socioeconomic costs of regulatory inaction.

Report Says There's Strong Evidence These Chemicals Harm Health

Humans and wildlife are exposed to a wide range of these chemicals, and the evidence linking exposure to diseases and disorders "is strong and continues to grow," the report says. People can be exposed through ingestion, skin absorption, inhalation, and direct contact with medical devices during procedures. Children can also be exposed by putting toys containing these chemicals in their mouths and through skin contact with the toys.

Prenatal and early-life exposure to EDCs affects neurodevelopment, cognition, and behavior; EDCs are linked to cancer, cardiovascular disease, obesity, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic liver disease, according to the report. Reproductive organs, fertility, and thyroid functions are also disrupted.

When the 2012 report was published, there was a lot of evidence these chemicals harmed health, but it was not necessarily pointing in the same direction at the same kind of health effects, said Laura Vandenberg, PhD, one of the lead authors for Tuesday's report. Vandenberg also contributed to the 2012 report.

Now, there's "essentially a statement of irrefutable evidence linking EDCs to human health effects and also environmental damage," said Vandenberg, a professor of environmental health sciences at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

People Are Exposed to These Chemicals Through Some Plastics

Some countries are pushing to regulate chemicals used to make plastics as part of the negotiations over a global treaty to end plastic pollution. This report empowers those countries that are pushing for controls, said Bjorn Beeler, international coordinator for the International Pollutants Elimination Network (IPEN).

Beeler said the amount of harm from these chemicals is only going to increase in future years as plastic and chemical production is projected to skyrocket -- a "toxic tidal wave" no one is prepared for. IPEN wants a treaty that places global controls on hazardous chemicals in plastics and ends the rapid growth of plastic production. Negotiations are set to resume early next year.

Chemical additives to plastics impart flexibility, rigidity, UV stabilization, durability, and other characteristics that help products perform as intended, said the American Chemistry Council (ACC), a trade group that represents the U.S. chemical industry. The industry considers the safe use of chemicals paramount, said Kimberly Wise White, PhD, ACC's vice president of regulatory and scientific affairs.

The plastics industry opposes efforts to impose new restrictions through the treaty, arguing that chemicals used in plastics are best regulated through existing international conventions and national laws that consider all of a chemical's uses. White said comprehensive frameworks, like the Toxic Substances Control Act in the U.S. and the European Union's Registration, Evaluation, Authorization, and Restriction of Chemicals regulation, that evaluate uses of a chemical to determine risk, are the most effective way to regulate plastic additives.

The International Council of Chemical Associations, which represents manufacturers and producers around the world, has contributed $1.65 million and provided technical expertise to help countries implement chemical management systems, as well as created a publicly accessible plastic additives database.

Few Chemicals Have Been Tested for Endocrine Disruption

More than 350,000 chemicals and chemical mixtures have been registered for production and use globally, but the vast majority have never been evaluated for endocrine-disrupting properties, the report says.

There has been more effort in recent years to develop testing programs, which were highlighted as a major need in the 2012 report. However, most of that testing has not led to action to regulate these chemicals and control exposure, Vandenberg said.

The take-home message from Tuesday's report, she said, is that "in many, many cases we know enough to act. Why haven't we acted?"

Chemicals have been removed from products when people become aware and stop buying products containing a certain chemical, like bisphenol A (BPA), which has been used to make plastic containers for storing food and beverages, Vandenberg said. But that can lead to a "whack-a-mole problem," where a substitution is created but it's structurally similar or insufficiently tested, she added.

To truly reduce people's exposures to these chemicals, it must be done at a policy level throughout society, Vandenberg said.

The report says regulators should aim to protect vulnerable populations from exposure, particularly during pregnancy, infancy, and childhood; improve monitoring and understanding of exposure to these chemicals; advance the identification and testing of them; account for the costs of exposure; and strengthen regulations, among other steps.

The estimate of the annual health-related costs is a conservative calculation that accounts for the cost of health treatment and lost productivity, the report says. The $1.1 trillion price tag doesn't account for the additional costs associated with contaminated drinking water, loss of biodiversity, impacts on food production, and even human rights.

Bethanie Carney Almroth, PhD, U.N. Special Rapporteur on toxics and human rights, said she hopes the report will spur action, though international cooperation is challenging.

"This report makes clear that new regulations are needed, new testing paradigms must be adopted," said Carney Almroth, an ecotoxicology professor at Sweden's University of Gothenburg. "We need to reverse responses from reactive to proactive. We need to prevent harm from occurring, rather than merely documenting and treating it after the fact."

#5647. BYD E6Y Odyssey

A couple of friends embark on a road trip to pick their EV purchase, and it turns into an Odyssey.

The BYD E6 is a BEV classic. Globe-trotting friends have ridden in them as taxis in Singapore. Majella and I even took one for a test drive (it reminded me of a ’70s Chrysler Valiant). It was the best selling pure electric car in China in 2016, with about 600,000 sold globally, and it is viewed by many as ahead of its time. So, when one showed up at our coffee and cake morning tea, I had to interview the owner, Joanne, and her road trip friend, Meredith. What they shared with me was truly an odyssey of determination to get Jo’s car home. Please note: this story took place 6 years ago. Charging availability has improved and so has Joanne’s knowledge of living with an electric vehicle.

Joanne told me that she had been looking for an EV for two years when a search on carsales.com found an ad for an E6Y (the taxi version of the BYD E6). It was a pre-COVID import and had been mothballed at Sydney airport after the company importing the vehicles had decided not to go ahead with taxis. Photos of all the BYDs at the airport were widely circulated as evidence that no one wanted to buy an EV. The cars were being “sold by a mate out of the back of the factory.” At the low cost of AU$32,000, claiming a 400 km range from its 83-kWh battery and only 100 km on the odometer, Joanne saw it as a bargain.

There was some consideration of putting the car on a flatbed and having it shipped, but in the end, the two friends decided on a road trip.

Jo informs me that: “They only brought 120 of the BYD E6Y taxi versions into the country. BYD sold some GLX versions, which had more bells and whistles.”

She was soon to find out that all is not as it seems. Her lack of knowledge of EVs meant that her trip in the car from Sydney back to Brisbane would be an odyssey of Greek tragedy proportions. Jo reminisces: “Meredith reminded me our original plan had been to spend just two days driving back to Brisbane with the one overnight stay. I thought I could ‘fast charge’ the car and make it back to Brisvegas on the second day. Hahahaha. Lesson learned the hard way.” They expected it to be just a twelve-hour trip. Meredith adds, “I told her we would laugh about it one day.”

Joanne contacted the seller and planned her flight to Sydney. Meredith got excited and joined the “road trip” in Newcastle. Jo paid the money and took ownership of the car. “It took two hours to get out of Sydney.” To be fair, that wasn’t the car’s fault — just Sydney’s congested traffic. However, the fact that the previous owner had only charged the car to 50% didn’t help. She was able to charge the car to 80% on the outskirts of Sydney. “But I had no idea that I wouldn’t get the expected range at highway speeds.”

Another learning curve was the state of charging points — sure, there were plenty listed on PlugShare, but many were unavailable or broken. Again, dear reader, I must emphasize this was 6 years ago.

Her next planned stop was accommodation she had booked at Newcastle. She got to within 2 km when the battery readout said “zero.” She was unable to find a place to charge — the car had not come with a granny charger. Jo clarified her Newcastle experience by email: “the Uni in Newcastle was the first I tried to charge. My friend Meredith and I tried three other places to charge all with no luck. I found out later that the Newcastle chargers were notorious for not working.” She confided to me that she now knows that the car can go a little further even when it says zero battery. She also had to learn the difference between AC and DC charging. The BYD she had bought could only handle AC charging.

With the battery reading zero, she felt she had no choice but to leave the car at a nearby garage. The owner of the accommodation she had booked kindly came and picked her and her friend up. The next day, the BNB owner dropped them back to the garage and a tow truck was ordered. The tow truck took them and their car to a local winery where they trickle charged next to the golf carts. The winery also had a Tesla level 2 charger for customer use. It was charging when they arrived. “We left a note on the windscreen of the Tesla that was using the level 2. During breakfast the Tesla owner rang and said the charger was available. We left the winery fully charged and off up the highway.” Not a bad place to get stuck, methinks.

280 km up the road to Kempsie, there was access to free charging in the council carpark, but no available accommodation! That’s what happens when you travel on the Queen’s Birthday long weekend. “We were checking out the back seat of the car as a place to sleep when a friend of a friend told them he had a farm in area. ‘Have I got a place for you!’ he told them. After we finished charging, we had to drive down this dark farm track. We couldn’t plug the car in because we still didn’t have a granny charger!” They made themselves comfortable in the available beds in the barn. The next morning in the light of day they found they had driven alongside of a lagoon! “We could have easily driven into that!”

Meredith adds: “I didn’t think I’d be sleeping in a shed with a tractor and then I couldn’t sleep because of the smell of diesel.” The trip was not just a challenge, but torture.

Their next adventure was just a few kilometers up the road at Gladstone NSW. Low on juice, they contacted people through PlugShare and got a message from a local café owner. You can check out the café here. He already owned a Hyundai Ioniq, and so had a granny charger to lend. The café owner knew a fellow who was visiting his mum in town. This friend had ordered an Atto 3 from BYD and was waiting on this first shipment of BYDs to arrive. Jo took him for a ride around town in her car. “This was his first ride in a BYD.”

He arranged for them to leave their car at his mother’s home in the next town (Smithtown). Jo and her friend were now in a hurry, as both had to get back to Brisbane to go to work the next day. Leaving the car charging, “We belted back to Brisbane in this horrible little roller skate hire car.” Home in Brisbane, Jo had to plan how to retrieve her BYD purchase. Meredith did not want another “road trip.”

This time, Jo travelled south by train. Even this trip was not without drama. She missed her stop. Thankfully, she was able to get off at the next stop and change to the northbound train to make it back to where her car waited faithfully for her. She took a taxi to her car, returned the borrowed granny charger, and began her journey home. She was so keen that she ended up with a speeding ticket.

Joanne arrived at her motel in Balina with 10 km of range showing on the dashboard. But the available ocular charger soon filled up the car. By 9:00 pm, with a full battery, she couldn’t wait to go home. The fireworks display in town was a fitting sendoff for the final leg of her journey.

Jo would like to acknowledge all the good advice and offers of help she received from fellow users of PlugShare, as well as all those referred to above. She is now a confident and competent driver of her BYD E6Y and has made many trips back and forth to Sydney from Brisbane with less drama. The BYD E6Y Facebook group has been a great help. She says she would not part with her green E6Y Singapore taxi — “a comfortable and solid basic car.” Rumour has it that there are about 250 on Australian roads, with the record distance travelled over 1 million km.

Another owner commented: “This unstoppable tank will outlive me I’m sure, best of all its super basic … no internet, no lane assist, no self-driving and plenty of new and used cheap parts available. This is why it seems like there are so few … they are so good NO ONE who has one is selling them.”

Jo has even taken her car camping. “The camping trip was to Yandina up the coast. I did sleep in the back of the car on that trip very comfortably. But that time I had a mattress and bedding. I did take out the bottom half of the back seat from the car so I could get a completely flat rear area for the mattress. When I returned from the camping trip, I popped the rear seat bottom back in the car. It’s just two bolts and a couple of plastic clips that hold it in.”

And in the future, I asked? “It will be hard to part with my E6. I am waiting on the first solid state 1000km BEVs before I would consider parting with it. I just love the two-tone paint job.”

Jo is another happy battery electric vehicle owner, sharing her learning experience “odyssey” and having fun. “Thanks for the opportunity to immortalise the odyssey,” she told me in her latest email. The future is bright and electric as we learn to live with our new vehicles.

David Waterworth is a retired teacher who divides his time between looking after his grandchildren and trying to make sure they have a planet to live on. He is long on Tesla [NASDAQ:TSLA].

#5646. 1969 Chevy Camaro SS For Sale With 10,000 Miles Shown Boasts 396 V8 And Body-Up Restoration

While we're yearning for another generation of the legendary Chevrolet Camaro, our best bet is to look back at its golden era — and one of the most pristine restomods we've found on Hemmings. This Ontario orange 1969 Camaro SS, listed by a Clarkston, Michigan dealer for $58,900, shows 10,000 miles on the odometer and a body-up restoration. Its 396 big-block raises a fair question: How did that engine really stack up against its rivals back in '69?

Neither the Hemmings listing nor the dealer's YouTube walkaround gives horsepower or torque figures, but this clearly isn't a stock motor. The 396 wears an Edelbrock Performer aluminum intake, ceramic headers, a mild camshaft, and a Flame Thrower high-energy-ingition distributor, with chrome valve covers and an air cleaner on top. Behind it, a Turbo-Hydramatic 400 automatic sends power to a 10-bolt rear axle with 3.23 gears.

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j-bnQtJsNGQ]

For context, Chevrolet offered three 396s in the 1969 SS, rated at 325, 350, and 375 horsepower, with torque between 410 and 415 pound-feet. The 375-horsepower L78 sat at the top, peaking at 5,600 rpm. So without a dyno sheet, there's no telling where this restomod example lands among them.

On paper, the L78 outgunned most of its competition. Its 375 horsepower beat the 345 claimed for Pontiac's Ram Air IV Firebird or the 335 rated for Mustang Mach 1's 428 Cobra Jet — one of the most powerful powertrains the Mach 1 ever came with. Even the base 325-horsepower SS 396 sat within 10 horsepower of the Cobra Jet.

Testing was less flattering. Car Life's figures (per Curbside Classic), recorded in showroom-stock trim, have a Camaro SS 396 L78 reaching 60 mph in 6.8 seconds and covering the quarter-mile in 14.77 seconds at 98.7 mph. The Mach 1 428, meanwhile, managed 5.5 seconds and 13.9 at 103.3 mph. Two other 375-horsepower rivals also ran quicker quarter-miles: the Plymouth 'Cuda 440 at 14.01 seconds, and the Boss 429 Mustang at 14.09, despite a slower 7.1-second run to 60. Traction was the usual culprit, since bias-ply tires struggled with big-block torque, so gross ratings didn't settle the pony car argument.

The Camaro's paint is Ontario orange metallic with a black hockey stripe, and there are front and rear spoilers, a cowl hood, and dual chrome mirrors. The 17-inch American Racing Torque Thrust wheels are wrapped in Dunlop 255/45ZR17 tires in back and 235/40R17s up front. The car also gets tubular upper and lower control arms, an aluminum radiator, power steering, and power front discs with slotted and drilled rotors. Inside, the black vinyl interior includes factory bucket seats, a center console, a sport steering wheel, and a Retrosound radio. So while we speculate on the return of the Camaro, consider looking to the past to get the edge off with this low-mile time capsule.

#5645. FDA Wants Liquid Statin Off Shelves

— Missing annual reports put simvastatin oral suspension on thin ice

The FDA wants a liquid formulation of simvastatin (FloLipid) withdrawn from the market, though the agency is giving the drugmaker an opportunity for a hearing.

Approval of simvastatin oral suspension is at risk because Salerno Pharma "has repeatedly failed to file required annual reports" to the FDA, according to a notice in the Federal Register.

According to FDA policy, these annual reports are supposed to convey labeling information and technicalities, such as a current list of approved chemistry, manufacturing, and control information.

Initially approved in 2016 for a host of indications, simvastatin oral suspension is marketed as the first LDL cholesterol medication in liquid form for U.S. patients. The product was developed for patients who have difficulty swallowing pills, and the recommended usual starting dose is 10 mg or 20 mg once a day in the evening on an empty stomach.

Regarding safety, an increased risk of myopathy, including rhabdomyolysis, has been observed in patients taking an 80-mg dose of the oral suspension. Other patients unable to hit their LDL cholesterol goal taking the 40-mg dose are advised to initiate alternative LDL cholesterol-lowering treatments. In 2020, the drug label for the liquid simvastatin formulation was updated with a warning of rare reports of immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy associated with statin use.

According to the Federal Register notice -- which came from Michael Davis, MD, PhD, the FDA's top drug regulator -- Salerno is being given a shot at requesting a hearing if it wants to argue why the approval should not be withdrawn.

Salerno's simvastatin suspension was previously manufactured for Rosemont Pharmaceuticals, a Perrigo company.

Oral suspension atorvastatin (Atorvaliq) is an alternative liquid statin on the market.

FY 2027 Transportation Proposal Puts EV Charging Investments at Risk

WASHINGTON, D.C. — On Monday, Senate Republicans released an Appropriations package that proposes to take back nearly $2 billion in federal funding already allocated to states to build out electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and repurpose it for general transportation uses, putting critical clean transportation investments at risk.

Republicans already clawed back roughly $500 million from the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) Formula Program in the FY 2026 appropriations bill. Now, they are proposing to further divert these funds, even as all 50 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico have approved plans for their use and are working to deliver critical charging infrastructure to their communities. More than half of available NEVI funding has already been committed to projects, and the proposal threatens to upend additional awards that states continue to make to charging developers.

For example, Texas recently made an announcement of $226 million in awards that will support 321 stations. The Senate proposal would threaten Texas’s remaining NEVI funding, along with funding for states like Ohio, which has one of the largest numbers of operational NEVI-funded stations in the country.

In response, Clean Transportation for All Director Katherine García released the following statement:

“It is unacceptable for Senate Republicans to once again seek to claw back critical EV charging investments. Trump’s day-one freeze of NEVI set states back, and they are only now back on track after we successfully challenged that freeze in court. This latest proposal threatens affordable transportation for American families, clean air for communities, and states’ efforts to build the infrastructure of the future. We have successfully defended NEVI against the Trump administration’s attacks, and we will continue fighting to protect the program and ensure these investments reach communities across the country.”

The NEVI program, established through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law in 2021, provides funding to states to build a nationwide network of EV fast-charging stations. Protecting that investment is essential to expanding charging access, supporting EV adoption, reducing dependence on volatile gasoline prices, and cutting transportation pollution.

Since the Trump administration’s unlawful freeze of the NEVI program was lifted following successful litigation by Sierra Club, its partners, and a coalition of states, hundreds of millions of dollars in NEVI funding have been committed to charging projects.

Congress must preserve funding for EV charging infrastructure while providing dedicated resources for passenger rail, public transit, and other clean transportation priorities.

The Sierra Club is America’s largest and most influential grassroots environmental organization, with millions of members and supporters. #5643. Mercedes Is Auctioning Off A C111 For The First Time Ever, And It'll Be Your Last Chance To Buy One For At Least 25 Years

Back in 2022, Mercedes-Benz brought a chosen group of collectors to its Museum for a secret auction, at which one of the two 1955 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupés was sold for a record-breaking €135 million, about $143 million according to exchange rates at the time. Most people, myself including, thought there was no way Mercedes would have ever sold one of the Uhlenhauts, not to mention many of the other slightly less rare and iconic cars in its collection. Now that it had auctioned off its most valuable car, it opened up so much speculation: What could be next?

Turns out the next thing is another completely unexpected sale. On Tuesday night, at an event kicking off the week's Rétromobile New York festivities, Mercedes-Benz announced that in just a few months it will be selling one of its groundbreaking C111 prototypes. This will be the first time Mercedes has ever sold a C111, and unlike the Uhlenhaut, it will be a public auction held at RM Sotheby's Rétromobile Paris sale in February, with all proceeds going towards funding the future of the Mercedes-Benz Museum.

While I don't think the C111 will touch the Uhlenhaut's record hammer price, you really should never say never. There's no precedent for how much this car could go for, especially given that Mercedes-Benz has promised it won't sell or auction off another C111 for at least 25 years. If you want one, now might be your only chance, and the C111 in question is perhaps the best one of the bunch.

As a bit of a memory refresher, the first C111 was introduced to the public at the 1969 International Motor Show in Frankfurt, though a few were already built by then, and an updated version was shown the following year in Geneva. It was strictly an experimental vehicle, a testbed for future technology, design and powertrain ideas. Prospective customers handed Mercedes blank checks to get a C111 of their own, and Mercedes says there was "enormous public interest," but the C111 was never put into production. The company cites the 1973 oil crisis, new emissions standards and high production costs as the reasons why, but that didn't stop Mercedes from continuing to build more new versions.

Between 1969 and 1978, Mercedes built 17 different C111s across three iterations of the model: the C111-I, the C111-II, and the C111-III. The C111 was originally conceived with a rotary powertrain, first a three-rotor Wankel with later versions getting a four-rotor engine. One was built with a V8 and another has since been converted to have a V8, and the last few C111-IIIs had five-cylinder turbodiesels with which they set a bunch of records at Nardò. Three of the C111s were dismantled after testing, and one was destroyed in crash testing; the rest have remained in Mercedes' collection ever since, with only a couple of them being still functional.

As Mercedes continued building new iterations of the C111, the overall design and various details evolved, but every C111 was spectacular and clearly part of the same family. The company had never made a mid-engined sports car, not to mention anything such a wild wedge shape, so it's no surprise they were show-stoppers everywhere. Some C111s had their glass-fiber-reinforced plastic bodywork originally painted white, and the last few were metallic silver, but the cars are best known for the Weißherbst paint worn by the vast majority of them — "white autumn" in German, named after a traditional copper-tinted rosé.

The C111 being sold is a C111-II, car number 33, which Mercedes says is "only of internal significance." Production began in March 1970 with the car being completed in August, when it became the second C111-II to go into the test fleet. It was fitted with a 2.4-liter four-rotor Wankel engine that produced a massive 345 horsepower and 289 pound-feet of torque, sending the 2,734-pound car from 0 to 62 mph in 4.8 seconds and on to a top speed of 186 mph (300 km/h), making it the fastest car in the world at the time. In fact, chief test engineer Hans Liebold once hit 188 mph on the Autobahn heading towards Baden-Baden.

Mercedes says Car 33 "was used to test a fluidic component designed to ensure even emptying of the two side fuel tanks, which have a combined capacity of 30.6 gallons, to carry out temperature measurements in the rear trunk, and to conduct test drives at the Hockenheimring." It was featured on the first German issue of Playboy in 1972, and since 1975 it has been retired, part of Mercedes-Benz's collection. When the museum opened in 2006, the car has been on display in the Fascination Design area, floating on a plinth surrounding a curved staircase.

In 2024, the Mercedes-Benz Classic team in Fellbach gave Car 33 a full restoration, making it one of just a couple C111s that actually still run, and the only running car with a rotary engine. The mechanical restoration was completed without messing up the car's lovely patina, the only addition to the car being a fire extinguisher. It has the original paint and houndstooth cloth seats, and a Becker Europa radio that actualy works.

There are 24,766 kilometers on the odometer (about 15,389 miles), and Mercedes says that while Car 33 was used to test anti-lock braking systems, the ABS currently doesn't work. The car comes with its original magnesium racing wheels, sized 10x15-inch in front and 13x15-inch in the rear, but they are "not only suitable for display purposes," so Mercedes created a new set of 8x15 light alloy wheels that the car can actually be driven on. The rear trunk tub, which is designed to hold luggage, is fitted and able to be removed.

I'm particularly excited to see how much this car goes for because I've had a few very special experiences with C111s, including this specific one. Mere days before the world shut down in 2020, I was given a tour of Mercedes' secret "holy halls" warehouses in Germany, where I saw half of all the C111s all lined up together. (The photo you see below, which Mercedes graciously let me take on a film camera.)

At Monterey Car Week in 2022 I got to ride shotgun the V8-powered C111 on the Tour d'Elegance, which was incredible even when we were stuck in traffic and slightly overheating. In 2024, I got to ride up and down Big Sur in this particular car, number 33, fresh off its restoration with a fully functioning rotary engine. The V8 C111 already felt extraordinary, but the four-rotor motor's totally unique buzzy sound and character really takes it to the stratosphere. There's no other car in existence quite like it.

Apart from other C111s, of course. Yes, it's pretty nuts that Mercedes is selling one of these things, but it will still have 12 others in the collection. I'm sure now that the Classic team got this one working, it will be able to restore one of the other rotary-powered C111s in the collection. Don't think this is the last the world will see of this C111, either. Part of the buyer contract for the Uhlenhaut was that its new owner must bring the car to events and shows, and that Mercedes gets to use it for things when it wants, and I'm sure the same will be the case for this sale.

Whoever buys it really should use it, too. For all of its fantastical styling and engineering, it's a proper car. Sure, the rotary doesn't really like sitting around at low speeds, instead egging you on to keep reaching the red mark at 7,000 rpm on the tachometer, and there's no air conditioning so your only respite from in-cabin heat is to open the small vent windows (or just open the gullwing doors). It's pretty comfortable, though, and pretty easy to get in and out of. The engine isn't so loud that you can't hold a conversation with your passenger, and the interior just feels like any other Mercedes from the '70s.

The C111 be will be sold on February 3, 2027, at the Salles du Carrousel underneath the Louvre, where RM Sotheby's typically has its Rétromobile auction. RM Sotheby's says bids can be placed by phone or in person at the auction, after reigstering ahead of time of course, and if you're interested you can go to the Mercedes Classic Center website to learn about "the terms and conditions of participation, bidder registration and opportunities for pre-inspection." Given the C111's existence as a forward-thinking experiment, I think it's fitting that the money goes toward making the automaker's museum even better for future generations. Says Mercedes:

The aim of "Mercedes-Benz Museum 2.0" is to bring the brand's unique heritage to life for future generations and make it accessible worldwide. To this end, Mercedes-Benz is continuously developing both the Museum in Stuttgart and its virtual offerings. A key component is the Museum's digital twin. This makes the Museum experience accessible regardless of physical location, thereby extending its reach far beyond Stuttgart. It will give people all over the world greater access to the Mercedes-Benz brand heritage. The virtual twin is being developed in collaboration with The Classic Car Trust (TCCT) and its digital platform, Roarington.

"With 'Mercedes-Benz Museum 2.0' , we are consistently taking our Museum to the next level. We are continuing to write our company and brand history right up to the present day, creating new exhibition experiences and providing space for topics that are of particular interest to our visitors – from more recent classic cars to the latest innovations. With a digital twin, we are also opening up the Museum to people all over the world. Visitors can also experience the exhibits interactively here. The first results will be visible as early as 2027." -Bettina Haussmann, Director of the Mercedes-Benz Museum

So, how much could it go for? Who the hell knows. The collector car market is so absurd these days — McLaren F1s are $35-million cars now — and there's no prior sales of cars that you can really compare the C111 to. Last year the Indianapolis Motor Speedway auctioned off a Mercedes-Benz W196 R race car that become the second-most-expensive sale ever, also in parnership with the automaker and RM Sotheby's. The most expensive public sale of a Ferrari 250 GTO has been just under $52 million, while private sales have been rumored to exceed $70 million, and I think the C111 could easily clear that mark.

For its part, Mercedes says that "for at least 25 years, this will remain the only opportunity: Mercedes-Benz has contractually committed not to sell any further C111s during this period." That's definitely an incentive for people to keep raising their paddles. I'm also going to take this sale as confirmation that Mercedes is definitely working on a C111-inspired supercar in the vein of the Vision One-Eleven concept from a few years ago.

#5642. Zoox Partnering with Uber to Bring Autonomous Mobility to More Riders

Now live in Las Vegas, with Los Angeles to follow

In March 2026, we announced a multi-year partnership between Zoox and Uber to bring our robotaxi experience to Uber’s growing autonomy platform in select cities.

Now, beginning today, Uber riders in Las Vegas will have the opportunity to be matched with a Zoox robotaxi on eligible trips. Zoox will also continue to offer rides through the Zoox app. In addition, Zoox and Uber are the official robotaxi and rideshare partners of MGM Resorts’ Las Vegas properties. Together, they’re working with MGM Resorts to make pickups and drop-offs easier and more intuitive, with improved on-property wayfinding, in-app guidance, and infrastructure improvements designed to support smoother traffic flow.

The Zoox purpose-built robotaxi gives riders the agency to create a space all their own, with design elements for enhanced socialization and safety not possible in a traditional car. Bringing this experience to Uber will help introduce the benefits of purpose-built autonomy to new, curious riders.

Within the Zoox and Uber apps, riders can take a Zoox to popular resorts and venues on and around the Strip, as well as rides in the Downtown & Arts District. More destinations will be added soon.

We will continue to offer our service through the Zoox app, in addition to rides being available through Uber in those cities.

Zoox was founded in 2014 on a bold belief: if you’re going to reinvent mobility, you have to start from scratch. Instead of retrofitting cars with autonomous technology, we designed the world’s first purpose-built robotaxi: fully autonomous, all-electric, bidirectional, and intentionally engineered around the rider experience. Since the very beginning, we’ve been focused on our vision of delivering safe and enjoyable mobility.

Like Zoox, Uber was founded in San Francisco with a vision to improve urban transportation. Uber started in 2010 as a ridehail app connecting riders with cars, but quickly evolved. Over the past decade, it expanded into shared rides, food delivery, freight logistics, micromobility, and is now building an autonomous vehicle network, consistently redefining how people and goods move through the world. By leveraging smartphone technology, dynamic pricing, and real-time data, Uber helped catalyze the on-demand economy and reshape how people get from A to B on a global scale. This partnership is a testament to Uber’s dedication to advancing transportation within the ridehail space.

Zoox has always taken a measured, step-by-step approach by starting small, learning quickly, and scaling responsibly. This launch with Uber mirrors that approach. We’re beginning with a small fleet with the potential to expand as we refine our operations, technology, and customer experience.

Uber and Zoox will launch in Los Angeles next year, after Zoox opens service on the Zoox app.

#5641. Peanut Peptide Injections Promising for Allergy Immunotherapy

— A novel route to immunotherapy for peanut allergy passes phase II test

A novel peptide-based immunotherapy for peanut allergy appeared safe and modestly efficacious for reducing children's symptoms over the first 12 months, a phase II trial showed.

For the primary efficacy endpoint, the higher of two monthly PVX108 shot dosages significantly boosted the maximum tolerated dose of peanut from baseline to month 12 by 2.4-fold, compared with a 1.2-fold change in the placebo group, reported Brian P. Vickery, MD, of Emory University and chief of the Division of Allergy/Immunology at Children's Healthcare of Atlanta, at the American College of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology annual meeting.

In terms of safety, there were no cases of anaphylaxis or other treatment-related allergic or severe adverse events with the shot. Only six of the 71 trial participants reported any adverse event (13% with the higher dose tested), largely local administration site reactions.

At an oral food challenge at 1 year, 39% of patients on the higher dose tolerated at least 300 mg of peanut protein compared with 17% in the placebo group (the equivalent of one peanut). "This is more than double, on average, what causes accidental reactions in the field when people are exposed accidentally while they're trying to avoid peanut. And it's been shown in previous work that ... is probably clinically meaningful for most patients with peanut allergy," Vickery said. But he acknowledged it "is probably less than what you'd expect in a study of oral immunotherapy, where the participants are swallowing about 300 mg of protein daily as part of their treatment."

While efficacy needs to be confirmed in a larger trial, "there's also a big safety difference and a difference in burden in terms of daily versus monthly therapy," he added, pointing to adverse events in most immunotherapy patients with other routes of administration and anaphylaxis in 10-15% of trial participants in some studies.

Immunotherapy shots offer an advantage of fewer office visits than the typically once-every-2-week schedule for oral immunotherapy up-dosing and also not requiring kids to consume peanut products daily, commented Jay Lieberman, MD, of the University of Tennessee Health Science Center in Memphis. With peanut protein, though, "you can't do it the same way we do allergy shots to cat or oak tree pollen, because it is too dangerous. It caused too many reactions," he said.

PVX108 comprises seven short peptides representing immunodominant T-cell epitopes of major peanut allergens rather than intact peanut proteins that interact with the immune system and can lead to reactions. "This is designed to get around that problem by formulating fragments of peanut proteins that are too small to interact with IgE [immunoglobulin E] and the allergic components of the immune system and instead interact directly with T cells, which are thought to be kind of the driving force behind the allergy," Vickery said.

"We have made some progress in being able to treat peanut allergy with oral immunotherapy and now FDA-approved omalizumab [Xolair] as the two most commonly used options," Vickery said in an interview monitored by media relations for Children's Healthcare of Atlanta. "But there are millions of patients out there with peanut allergy, and most of them are not being treated due to limitations in care and also limitations in access to these treatments and because of limitations in the treatments themselves."

"The scientific community believes that there is plenty of room for new forms of immunotherapy to be developed," he added, "because we don't think of peanut allergy as a one-size-fits-all condition where one treatment will solve the problem."

While the only FDA-approved peanut oral immunotherapy product recently left the market as clinicians rely on off-the-shelf commercial products, Lieberman agreed that PVX108 could find a place: "Bringing an [oral immunotherapy] FDA-approved thing to the market when people are already just using PB2 powder [commercially available peanut flour], that was the problem."

The trial included 71 peanut allergy patients ages 4 to 11 years at 14 trial sites in the U.S. and Australia in the primary efficacy and safety cohort. They were randomized to double-blind treatment with 5-nmol or 50-nmol PVX108 or placebo given monthly by intradermal administration over 12 months. At the end of that period, a double-blind placebo-controlled food challenge was done following the PRACTALL guidelines.

After 6 months off treatment, a follow-up food challenge was conducted at month 18. It showed evidence of maintenance or improvement in clinical effects compared with month 12, indicating disease-modifying potential, Vickery said, although this needs further confirmation.

The optimal length of treatment isn't clear yet, but immunotherapy shots for other allergens typically take 3 to 5 years of treatment, Vickery noted. "So it's likely that longer-term treatment might be necessary or even might be more optimal."

Correction: The story has been corrected to state that media relations present for the interview with Vickery represented Children's Healthcare of Atlanta rather than drug developer Aravax.
