#5623. It's Official: U.S. Loses Measles Elimination Status After 25 Years

— Vaccine rates have fallen as cases rise

The U.S. has lost its measles-free status, international health officials said Tuesday, as the highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread -- largely among the unvaccinated -- at the highest rate in more than 30 years.

Mexico also lost its measles-elimination status, following a resurgence of the virus there that included a massive outbreak in Chihuahua state. Bolivia, too, lost its status.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) declaration has few practical implications and is largely symbolic, but it marks a sharp turnabout in a disease largely controlled through decades of scientific advances. It also may be seen as the beginning of an era in which diseases of the past become deadly problems for the modern world.

"Measles elimination is not a trophy that is won once and placed on a shelf," Jarbas Barbosa, MD, MPH, PhD, PAHO's director, said at a news conference. "It is an achievement that must be safeguarded every day by closing immunity gaps and ensuring we reach every community."

PAHO expects the U.S., Bolivia, and Mexico to submit plans "in the coming weeks" for how each country will go about trying to stop transmission for at least a year and regain measles elimination status, Daniel Salas, MD, the organization's executive manager for immunizations, told reporters.

Measles has been spreading throughout the Americas since 2024. The outbreaks in North America started in close-knit Mennonite communities and have since spread to areas with low vaccination rates. Last year, Canada lost its measles-free designation for the first time since 1998.

International health officials consider measles eliminated when the virus is not locally spreading among residents. The designation hinges on whether a single measles chain has spread uninterrupted for at least 12 months.

Tuesday's announcement signals an erosion of public health preparedness.

Vaccination rates have been falling against a number of diseases, in the U.S. and globally. And as one of the most infectious diseases known to medicine, measles was seen as likely to be one of the first vaccine-preventable diseases to reemerge when vaccinations falter.

That means others are likely to follow, some experts said.

"It can be the canary in the coal mine to other things," said Susan Kansagra, MD, chief medical officer of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials.

Measles vaccines have safely stopped the virus' spread in the U.S. for 30 years.

It takes a community vaccination rate of 95% to prevent outbreaks, experts say. But as fewer parents vaccinate their children and federal leaders sow doubt and confusion about the importance of getting vaccinated, the virus has found footholds in communities across the U.S. All but three states have reported a confirmed case of measles this year.

The last 2 years have been the worst in a generation in the U.S., with more than 7,000 cases and 13 reported deaths. Nearly all of those people were either unvaccinated or didn't report whether they were vaccinated. More than 10% of those infected had to be hospitalized.

The illness typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it's one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults over age 30.

Ten measles-associated deaths have been reported in the U.S. this year, making it the deadliest in more than three decades. Health officials haven't released detailed information on each death, but at least five of the dead were children.

Major Outbreaks in Texas, Utah, South Carolina, and Pennsylvania

Since the U.S. eliminated measles in 2000, public health officials usually logged fewer than 200 cases a year, most of them tied to international travel.

But since 2025, measles has sickened thousands. It started with a major outbreak in the Southwest.

In Texas, more than 760 people got sick and two children died. In New Mexico, about 100 people got sick and one adult died. Then measles exploded in rural border towns in Arizona and Utah, followed by a major outbreak in South Carolina in the winter and spring that sickened nearly 1,000 people.

This year has been much worse -- the worst for measles cases since 1991. The more than 5,400 confirmed cases so far this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that dwarfed the earlier ones.

And the outbreak tallies are almost certainly an undercount, public health experts say.

Critics Say the U.S. Response Is Falling Short

U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before President Donald Trump appointed him to oversee federal health agencies.

Kennedy and other federal leaders have argued that vaccination rates were waning for years before Trump took office a second time, that measles is not an "American phenomenon," and that the U.S. government is handling measles better than other countries. In January, a CDC leader told reporters that the loss of the nation's elimination status would be the "cost of doing business" globally.

It's true that other countries are struggling with measles, and some also have lost their measles-elimination status. But public health experts and others say the outcome in the U.S. wasn't inevitable.

"This humiliating determination is the tragic yet predictable result of an ongoing campaign by grifters, quacks, and charlatans to put their own greed and self-worth ahead of the health and safety of children," said Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.).

The government has been taking some steps. In August and September, the CDC awarded $100 million to support state and local measles-response work. And Kennedy and CDC Director Erica Schwartz, MD, MPH, have made statements that vaccination is the best way to prevent measles from spreading.

"The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does," Schwartz said in a statement Tuesday. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities."

But state and local health officials say the cost is far higher and that the moment demands a louder federal voice -- and a bigger push for vaccinations -- than Kennedy and Schwartz are providing.

"When the people at the front of the room are not speaking loudly and frequently in support of vaccination, the program starts to falter. And that's what we're seeing in the U.S.," said Noel Brewer, PhD, a University of North Carolina public health professor who chairs a committee that presented an analysis of U.S. measles data to PAHO last week. "How many kids have to die before they start getting concerned?"

Some experts noted that neither Kennedy nor the CDC has scheduled a news conference to address their plans to fight measles. When the AP asked for Kennedy's reaction to the U.S. losing its measles-free status, an HHS spokesperson pointed to Schwartz's statement. During the PAHO news conference, the health department did issue a news release promoting the latest episode of Kennedy's online cooking show.

After hugely successful vaccination campaigns, the Americas became the first region in the world to be free of measles in 2016. Health officials estimate the measles vaccine prevented 6.2 million deaths in the Americas between 2000 and 2023.

Now, the entirety of North America faces the task of earning back the designation.

#5622. Waymo Abandons Highways Entirely After California Ban

Happy Wednesday! It's November 18, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift — your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition we're looking at Waymo leaving the U.S. highway system, and German far-right politicians cozying up to Elon Musk. We'll also look at Royal Enfield's sales, and Mercedes' plans to move more cars next year.

If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.

The great state of California banned Waymo's autonomous cabs from its highways, and the company has decided to comply above and beyond the letter of the law — withdrawing its cabs from all highways across the U.S., regardless of whether or not the California law applies. From Reuters:

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 17 (Reuters) – Alphabet's Waymo has halted operations of its robotaxis on US freeways, it said on ​Tuesday, after a California regulator barred its vehicles from ‌freeways in the state.

The California ban, which took ​effect last week, is a result of a series of ​incidents where Waymo robotaxis entered active construction zones, the California Department of Motor Vehicles said in a statement on Tuesday.

"The Department determined that ​Waymo's driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public ​safety," it said.

The company quickly pulled the robotaxis from all freeways after the ban. Great first step! Now get them off the surface streets too. Then I'll really get behind what you're doing.

Elon Musk is a fan of far-right political parties, regardless of where on Earth they are. Case in point, Musk — a South African and United States citizen— has long been a major backer of Germany's extreme AfD party. Now that party is reaching out to Elon Musk, in hopes that he'll give them more cash. From Reuters:

BERLIN, Nov 17 (Reuters) – The Alternative for Germany's Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the far-right party's first state premier, appealed to Elon Musk ​to establish a Tesla presence in Saxony-Anhalt on Monday, promising "business-friendly ‌conditions."

The billionaire entrepreneur endorsed the party multiple times during the 2025 federal election, using his social media platform X to broadcast a conversation with AfD chancellor candidate ​and party leader Alice Weidel a month before the vote.

Writing on X in English, Siegmund said Saxony-Anhalt would actively ​support Tesla's presence under an AfD-led government and welcomed the chance to personally meet with the Tesla CEO.

Will we see Elon move to Germany rather than stick around in the States? Almost certainly not, no. Will he continue to back the AfD, despite — or rather, because of — its stances on which humans deserve rights? You bet.

According to parent company Eicher Motors' latest disclosures, Royal Enfield sold 842,538 motorcycles between April and October 2026, an 18% increase over the same period last year. That's an additional 125,684 motorcycles in just seven months, or roughly 18,000 extra bikes every month.

Having ridden my fair share of Enfields, I see the appeal. They're just so well-built, so simple, and so cheap — what's not to like?

#5620. HLTH 2026: CVS Health, Cigna and Abridge collaborating with OpenAI to test computer-use agents

HLTH 2026: CVS Health, Cigna and Abridge collaborating with OpenAI to test computer-use agents" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

OpenAI is expanding computer-use agents for healthcare, enabling AI to navigate electronic health record systems, payer portals and other software to tackle repetitive and manual tasks.

Computer-use agents, also called computer-using agents, are AI systems designed to interact with software interfaces the same way a human does—by viewing a screen, moving a cursor, clicking buttons and typing text.

Research teams at OpenAI have been exploring how computer-use agents can assist healthcare teams with fragmented clinical and administrative workflows while keeping people in control, Karan Singhal, head of Health AI and Artificial General Intelligence at OpenAI, told Fierce Healthcare.

"Around six months ago we set a research bet that we thought that the abilities for agents to use computers would end up being helpful and reliable enough in healthcare to help people with clinical and administrative workflows," Singhal said in an exclusive interview sharing evaluation results on OpenAI's early work with computer-use agents in healthcare.

In an interview with Fierce Healthcare, Singhal also shed light on how OpenAI is working with CVS Health, Cigna Healthcare, Abridge and Ambience to apply computer-use agents to specific workflows, including referrals, prior authorizations, discharge planning, specialist consults and care manager preparation.

Healthcare systems are often disconnected, forcing administrative staff and care teams to manually move information from one system to another before a patient can get care. If a clinician orders an MRI, for example, the insurer may need information from the patient’s medical record, but a staff member still has to pull that information and enter it into a separate portal to request authorization, Singhal noted.

OpenAI executives and researchers framed computer use as the next step in healthcare AI, moving beyond copilots that draft or summarize information to agents that can actually work across EHRs, payer portals and other applications on a user's behalf.

Computer-use agents can bridge healthcare's fragmented software environment, especially where application programming interfaces (APIs) and other integrations don't exist or don't connect an entire workflow, Singhal noted.

"We have been working with health systems on things like ChatGPT for Healthcare and our integration with Epic, but there are still limitations in how useful AI agents can be today. Computer use is really a way of resolving a lot of these barriers that exist between AI capabilities and healthcare software so that care teams can deliver better care, more effectively and more efficiently," he said.

OpenAI continues to invest in APIs, plugins and MCP connectors to integrate AI with healthcare software, but the industry’s fragmented and legacy technology can make those integrations slow and incomplete, Singhal said. Computer use can help bridge those gaps.

"What we hope to do with this release is move us closer to a world where, because AI is connected to more services, AI can help more with a lot of these workflows," he noted.

Care teams, developers and individual clinicians can access computer use for healthcare through ChatGPT for Healthcare, ChatGPT for Clinicians and the OpenAI API.

In a research demonstration using synthetic patient data, OpenAI showed how a computer-use agent could support a clinician and an authorization specialist working on the same MRI request. In the demonstration video, a patient messages their clinician about lower back pain. The clinician then instructs the computer-use agent to review the patient’s visit notes, physical therapy records and prior imaging in the EHR. The computer-use agent drafts an MRI order, an encounter note and a reply to the patient for the clinician to review.

In the same demo video, the agent then uses the same records to prepare a prior authorization request in the insurer’s portal for an authorization specialist to review.

"The clinician and authorization specialist were both completely in control of their workflow, but the computer-use agent was able to help across different parts of the workflow and translate that into action," Singhal noted about the demo video.

OpenAI evaluated GPT‑6 Astra on tasks clinicians handle in their EHR inboxes. These tasks, shaped by physician input, require Astra to carry out multi-step workflows designed to test both clinical reasoning over longitudinal patient context and navigation of complex interfaces. Reviewers examined the model’s actions alongside the notes, orders and patient messages it produced, assessing whether the work would be helpful and clinically safe in the context of the task, according to an OpenAI blog post.

OpenAI says its GPT-6 Astra model can perform multi-step EHR tasks such as reviewing patient records, drafting messages and notes, preparing medication refills and proposing orders, while leaving key actions for clinician review. In OpenAI's evaluation, 99% of 325 reviewed tasks were rated clinically safe, while physicians rated the model "very helpful" or "extremely helpful" in 93% of 646 assessments.

Clinical safety was assessed by evaluating whether inaccuracies, omissions or actions in the model’s work could plausibly lead to patient harm, OpenAI said.

Regarding the 1% of tasks rated not clinically safe, Singal said researchers did not identify any cases where the model created a specific, plausible risk of patient harm. "In some cases, the model might overreach and might take an action without getting the proper sign-off or authorization," he said.

"The models are not perfect today, and what we're sharing is an update on research results where we're seeing this critical point where the models seem to be useful in practice," he added.

OpenAI researchers also evaluated computer-use agents for administrative tasks, such as prior authorizations, appeals and medical equipment orders.

OpenAI says it designed its computer-use agents with robust safeguards and data security in place, according to the company. The agents can be configured with limits on system access and actions, and audit logs provide a clear record of agent actions and approvals, giving healthcare teams visibility into how each workflow was completed.

Organizations are testing out and deploying computer-use applications across different workflows and administrative tasks.

CVS Health is using OpenAI’s computer-use capabilities to automate repetitive work across clinical systems, including sending documents, processing referrals and supporting specialist consults. In one production workflow, an agent cleared a months-long document-sending backlog over a weekend, OpenAI detailed in the blog post. Another agent handles the system steps for tens of thousands of consults each day.

Generative AI company Abridge is building computer-use agents to help clinicians carry out care plans across use cases and applications they use every day, including those without APIs. The company also plans to develop an inpatient use case, adding EHR information and nurse and clinician context to identify what needs attention and to coordinate next steps, the company said. As an example, agents can work concurrently on medication access and home health coordination, using computer interaction alongside calls and messages.

Cigna Healthcare is using OpenAI’s models to pull together member information from more than 10 clinical and administrative systems, including benefits, providers, appointments and previous interactions. The goal is to reduce the time case managers spend searching across systems and give them more time to support members, OpenAI wrote in the blog post.

Companies including Assort, Bunkerhill, Forus, Gravity and Tennr are testing agents that interact directly with EHRs and payer portals for referral management, authorization checks, medication approvals and other operational tasks.

“We're continuing to invest in the models, making the models better at computer use. An important way that we think that they could continue to improve is around improved latency and costs,” Singhal noted.

OpenAI sees its role in healthcare as building foundational AI capabilities and letting healthcare companies handle the “last mile” of implementation, Singhal noted. Computer use is one example: OpenAI provides the technology and safeguards, while partners apply it to specialized workflows and deploy it within healthcare organizations.

The company also announced today improvements to trusted clinical search in ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians, including how ChatGPT finds, evaluates and cites medical evidence. OpenAI also expanded its healthcare plugin ecosystem with more than 20 new healthcare plugins from companies across clinical care, care coordination and business operations.

#5619. AI Writes Better Discharge Summaries Than Doctors, Study Suggests

— Physician reviewers gave AI summaries higher marks for accuracy, completeness, clarity, and tone

Artificial intelligence (AI) outperformed clinicians in drafting hospital discharge summaries, a U.K.-based retrospective study showed.

A higher proportion of large language model (LLM)-generated discharge summaries were signed off by a clinician reviewer with no or minor changes compared with clinician-authored summaries (92.2% versus 70.0%), meeting prespecified noninferiority criteria, reported Kathleen Goldsmith, MSc, senior data scientist at a partnership between Imperial College London and Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust in the U.K., and colleagues.

Moreover, clinician reviewers rated LLM-generated summaries higher on accuracy, completeness, tone, and clarity compared to clinician-written summaries, they wrote in JAMA Network Open.

Finally, a smaller proportion of AI-generated discharge summaries contained inaccurate or incomplete information compared with ones written by clinicians (26.2% vs 45.1%), they reported.

"Together, these findings suggest that AI-assisted documentation could strengthen the quality of information transferred at discharge, an important component of safe and effective continuity of care," Goldsmith told MedPage Today.

While this research focused on discharge summaries, Goldsmith said it could be applied to other administrative tasks, but "patient safety and clinical value have to be central to how we adopt technology like this."

In an accompanying editorial, Melanie Molina, MD, of the University of California San Francisco, wrote that this research raises the question not of whether AI can produce acceptable drafts, but whether physicians can verify the information in real-time.

"Lengthy, complex, and fragmented clinical records create a verification paradox: the cases in which automated summarization is most valuable are often the cases in which verification is most difficult," Molina wrote, adding that emergency department care poses particular challenges.

Plus, AI tools have already evolved far beyond the model tested in this study, with newer, more sophisticated models less likely to hallucinate.

Molina argued that while this research shows that "a thoughtfully designed LLM pipeline can produce discharge summaries that clinicians prefer to routine documentation," this does not yet equate to a safer transition of care.

"The enduring clinical task will be ensuring that what it writes is true, complete, and actionable," she wrote.

Goldsmith and team sought to evaluate how AI tools could "free up clinician time for patient-facing care while maintaining clinical safety and accuracy" and to develop a framework for evaluating the use of LLMs in clinical settings.

This retrospective noninferiority study used Imperial Clinical Analytics, Research and Evaluation (iCARE) research data from a network of 5 hospitals in London from Sept. 1, 2022, to Sept. 30, 2023.

Discharge summaries written by clinicians and by GPT-4o mini were blindly reviewed by 12 resident physicians from the Imperial College Healthcare Trust. The primary outcome was clinician sign-off on the discharge summary with little to no edits. Goldsmith noted this endpoint reflects how the technology would be used in real-world settings.

"Having clinician input in both the co-design, use, and evaluation of healthcare AI technologies is crucial to ensure these systems are trusted, and truly deliver the benefits to clinical work," Goldsmith said.

Ultimately, there were 1,294 discharge summaries included, of which 649 were clinician-authored and 645 were LLM-generated.

Patients' median age was 46 and 56.6% were female. The median length of stay was 3 days. On average, each case required the review of 30 clinical documents, or about 4,000 words.

The researchers noted some limitations, including that de-identification may have removed clinically relevant information, that only one LLM was evaluated, and the retrospective study design; prospective assessments at the point of care are still needed.

It marked the launch by announcing its first portfolio company: Wrapt Health, which offers an automated tool that predicts likely missed medical appointments for early outreach and rescheduling. In line with Permanentech’s broader thesis, it was born from a TPMG physician’s experiences, validated within the medical group and so far scaled to 22 sites in Kaiser Permanente’s Northern California region.

“Our clinicians are continuously innovating and refining how we deliver care,” Kenneth Trauner, M.D., CEO of Permanentech and chief innovation officer at TPMG, said in a release. “Permanentech gives them a dedicated resource to rapidly turn their insights and creativity into scalable solutions that benefit both our patients and the wider health care community.”

Permanentech will be focused on technologies and AI-enabled tools addressing patient service, access and quality, TPMG said, with successful products also having the potential to improve “the economics of care delivery.” The business is structured “to move at the pace of the technology industry,” but has “a clear advantage” via its access to TPMG and Kaiser Permanente’s substantial footprint for deployment and validation, it said.

Those efforts will involve both home-grown tools and those developed by established or early-stage partners.

Strategic partnerships and joint ventures, meanwhile, will focus on co-development, clinical valuation and scaled deployment. Permanentech said the latter will begin with local deployments that are expanded to other TPMG sites when solutions “prove their value,” and could include additional strategic support as a partner company looks to advance their offering beyond TPMG.

Permanentech plans to add more portfolio companies and partnerships “in the coming months,” according to its announcement.

“For decades, our physicians have delivered high-quality, preventive care inside an integrated system where clinical expertise, data and incentives all point toward keeping people healthy,” Maria Ansari, M.D., CEO and executive director of TPMG, said. “Permanentech is our commitment to putting that ecosystem to work alongside the best technology from inside and outside our walls.”

Pleasanton, California-based TPMG is the country’s largest medical group, caring for 4.7 million Northern California members with about 10,000 physicians and nearly 47,000 nurses and support staff. It operates at 203 medical offices and facilities, as well as 21 hospitals.

#5617. Cancer History Tied to Severe Maternal Morbidity During Childbirth

— Deliveries among cancer survivors have increased in recent years

More cancer survivors are giving birth, and severe maternal morbidity was increased at delivery for both past survivors and current cancer patients, a cross-sectional study in the U.S. showed.

From 2016 to 2023, hospital deliveries increased from 30.1 to 45.6 per 10,000 for past cancer survivors (average annual percentage change [AAPC] 6.3%), while hospital deliveries for current cancer patients were relatively unchanged (7.0 to 7.4 per 10,000 deliveries, AAPC 0.2%), reported Koji Matsuo, MD, PhD, of the University of Southern California in Los Angeles, and colleagues in JAMA Network Open.

Compared with a severe maternal morbidity rate of 6.8 per 1,000 hospital deliveries for people without cancer, this rate was 11.9 per 1,000 deliveries for past cancer survivors (adjusted incidence rate ratio [IRR] 1.45, 95% CI 1.37-1.53) and 48.2 per 1,000 deliveries for current cancer patients (adjusted IRR 3.80, 95% CI 3.58-4.04).

Of note, the inpatient maternal mortality rate during the admission for hospital delivery was 14-fold higher for current cancer patients compared with those without cancer (273.0 vs 7.0 per 100,000 hospital deliveries; adjusted IRR 14.24, 95% CI 10.87-18.66).

"As cancer care and outcomes have improved and fertility preservation and assisted reproductive technology have become more widely available, pregnancy after cancer is an important issue in survivorship care for reproductive-aged individuals, including adolescent and young adult cancer survivors," wrote Matsuo and colleagues. "The increase in delivery hospitalizations among past cancer survivors in the U.S. may partly reflect these changes."

"These findings support the importance of preconception evaluation for cancer survivors and early referral to tertiary care centers with multidisciplinary teams, as currently recommended by multiple organizations," they added.

This study used national hospital discharge data from the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project's National Inpatient Sample, which approximates a sample of 20% of discharges from participating hospitals across 48 states and the District of Columbia.

Among 28,360,443 hospital deliveries, 0.4% were among past cancer survivors, less than 0.1% were among current cancer patients, and 99.5% were among women without a cancer diagnosis. Median age at delivery was 33, 32, and 29 years across the three groups, respectively.

Among past cancer survivors, thyroid cancer (22.3%) was the most frequent type of cancer diagnosis, followed by cutaneous melanoma (15.7%), breast cancer (11.7%), lymphoma (10.8%), uterine cervical cancer (6.6%), leukemia (4.2%), and ovarian cancer (3.6%).

The study's primary outcome was severe maternal morbidity at the time of delivery, with morbidity indicators restricted to those with a case-fatality rate of 1% or higher after an event. The most common were cardiac arrest or ventricular fibrillation, conversion of cardiac rhythm, heart failure or arrest during surgery or a procedure, and amniotic fluid embolism.

Rates of severe maternal morbidity at delivery varied by cancer type, with greater associations seen among survivors of leukemia and lymphoma, and more modest associations with breast, cervical, and thyroid cancers.

Most hospital deliveries (57.6%) for past cancer survivors were full term, while only 39.6% were full term for current cancer patients.

Matsuo and colleagues acknowledged that the study had several limitations. For instance, they pointed out that unmeasured confounding factors were possible since they did not have access to information on cancer stage, histologic type, familial cancer syndrome, treatment history, duration of remission, residual organ dysfunction, or detailed disease status.

Allina Health, Sutter Health notch Minn. AG's approval for $26B combination" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health's plans to combine have earned the blessing of Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, a key hurdle that paves the path for a Jan. 1, 2027 close.

The nonprofit systems and the attorney general's office announced Monday an oversight agreement replete with service line preservation requirements and $2.15 billion of promised capital investments. Their deal is set to create a 39-hospital cross-regional health system that would be a major player in Minnesota's increasingly concentrated healthcare market.

"My office has extensive authority to review healthcare transactions in Minnesota: we take it very seriously and with every review, we apply the lens of whether it will help you afford your life and live with dignity, safety and respect," Ellison said in the announcement. "At the end of our thorough review of the transaction between Sutter and Allina, I have determined it passes the public-interest test.”

Per the attorney general's office, the $2.5 billion be invested over five years to increase healthcare capacity in the state. That includes $150 million toward rural care, $50 million in workforce development and the scaling of virtual addiction therapy programs across the state.

The systems also agreed to maintain core services at rural locations for five years, to maintain reproductive and gender care for five years (as it complies with state and federal statute) and to continue Medicare participation and charity care. For Allina's workforce, they also agreed to retain all employees in good standing, honor all collective bargaining agreements and not enforce some noncompete agreements.

Ellison's office will enforce the five-year commitments via a 10-year period of oversight, which will include annual compliance reports from Sutter and Allina.

"In the context where the provision of healthcare everywhere is under serious financial strain and Allina is facing its own struggles, I appreciate that Sutter is entering Minnesota with a mindset of growth and an understanding that we cannot simply cut our way out of financial challenges and maintain Minnesota’s high standard of healthcare," Ellison said. "Sutter’s leadership has a history of delivering on growth and innovation and I look forward to their doing the same here."

Since the nonprofits announced their deal back in March, Minnesota and the Midwest have been the stage for substantial health system dealmaking. Sanford Health announced and closed its acquisition of North Memorial Health, while Essentia Health and HealthPartners in September shared new plans to combine and form an integrated 22-hospital organization.

Sutter and Allina, in a joint statement, thanked Ellison's office for the sign-off and said they plan to close their transaction on Jan. 1, 2027.

"From the beginning, our vision has been grounded in a simple yet powerful belief: people across Minnesota and western Wisconsin deserve a sustainable health system that provides access to high-quality, affordable health care when and where they need it," the statement reads. "With our combined capabilities and more than $2 billion in investment, we will expand access to care, improve affordability, enhance care team and patient experiences and accelerate high-impact research and innovation."

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health's pending combination took a step forward this week with the signing of a definitive agreement, the nonprofit systems announced Thursday.

The agreement locks in the plans shared earlier this year in a letter of intent—namely, that the cross-market deal would bring more than $2 billion of investment to Allina's markets and that the smaller system would become the "Upper Midwest Division of Sutter Health."

Now the organizations are left with securing state and federal regulatory approvals before the deal can close, which they expect to happen before the end of this year.

“This important milestone brings us one step closer to our goal of partnering to enhance care, support our teams and expand clinical capabilities and research as a strong, nonprofit health system,” Lisa Shannon, president and CEO of Allina Health, said in Thursday's announcement. “With our combined expertise, complementary strengths and aligned missions and visions, I am confident we will be well-positioned to meet the evolving needs of our patients and communities now and well into the future.

Should the deal close, the resulting organization would span 39 hospitals as well as more than 400 primary and specialty care sites that collectively see over 5 million patients annually. The organization would also employ 88,000 people, with 18,000 aligned physicians.

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health unveiled plans to join and form a 39-hospital, $26 billion nonprofit health system.

Allina would maintain its brand and regional headquarters but operate as the Upper Midwest Division of Sutter. Under that arrangement, Sutter is also committing $2 billion to bolster care access and patient experience investments in Allina’s Minnesota and western Wisconsin markets.

“This includes establishing new ambulatory and specialty care sites to fill care gaps and meet growing community needs, as well as recruiting more physicians and enhancing AI and digital health capabilities,” Sutter Health President and CEO Warner Thomas, who would maintain those titles should the deal close, said in the announcement. “Building on our complementary strengths and combined expertise, we will build a healthcare innovation engine that accelerates how ideas move from development and design into improving the health of patients and communities.”

The systems said they plan to complete due diligence and finalize terms for a definitive agreement “over the coming weeks and months,” targeting a close before the end of 2026 should regulatory reviews run smoothly. A representative for Allina described the structure of the proposed agreement as being similar to a member substitution but noted that the deal's final structure will be outlined in the pending definitive agreement.

Alongside the 39 hospitals, the resulting organization would include more than 400 primary and specialty care sites that collectively see over 5 million patients annually. The combination would also employ 88,000 people, with 18,000 aligned physicians.

Among the benefits of their proposed partnership, the systems led their announcement with the synergistic technical expertise of their organizations and surrounding communities: Sutter’s immersion in Northern California's artificial intelligence and platform development and Allina’s seat in the medtech and engineering hub of Minnesota.

“The proposed combined system will be uniquely positioned to be a national leader in digital and technological advancements that meaningfully improve patients’ and caregivers’ experiences, while continuing to provide the compassionate care their respective communities have relied on for decades,” the announcement reads.

Such efforts, outlined in the announcement, include AI and digital solutions that would reduce administrative burdens for caregivers along with more convenient appointment scheduling for patients via digital consumer tools.

More broadly, the organizations said they expect the combination will help the organizations bolster physician and clinician recruitment, improve patient affordability and grow their capabilities, “particularly in clinical centers of excellence.”

“We are incredibly excited for the opportunity to harness the collective strength of our two mission-driven organizations to make a difference in the lives of our patients, communities and care teams,” said Allina Health President and CEO Lisa Shannon, who would also maintain those titles in regard to the to-be-formed Upper Midwest Division. “As one nationally leading, locally committed nonprofit health system, we will be uniquely positioned to be at the forefront of innovation, building upon the expertise of our physicians, advanced practice providers, nurses and team members to chart a new path for healthcare.”

#5615. The Homeownership Gap Between Young and Old Americans Has Doubled—These Cities Reveal Why

The homeownership gap between younger and older Americans has more than doubled over the past four decades, with some of the nation's most expensive cities seeing the sharpest increases, according to a new report.

The analysis, from the Urban Institute, finds that nationally just 43% of households headed by adults aged 25 to 35 owned their homes in 2024, compared with 79% of those headed by adults 65 and older. The 35.8-percentage-point difference is more than twice the 17.5-point gap recorded in 1980.

But that divide pales in comparison to the gaping chasm in some of America's most expensive metropolitan areas. Between 1980 and 2024, the homeownership gap grew by 29 percentage points in Denver, 23 points in New York City, and 22 points in San Francisco, compared with 18.3 points nationally.

But those widening gaps also expose a deeper economic trade-off: The cities offering young Americans the greatest opportunities to earn more may be the very places preventing them from building wealth through homeownership

"The cities with the strongest labor markets tend to be the least affordable, so some will take the better job and rent indefinitely, giving up equity accumulation," explains Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com®. "Others will pass up higher-paying roles or move to cheaper, lower-opportunity markets in order to buy."

In 1980, younger households in Denver were nearly as likely as their older counterparts to own a home.

At the time, 55% of households headed by adults aged 25 to 35 owned their homes, compared with 67% of households headed by adults 65 and older.

By 2024, the younger group's homeownership rate had fallen to just 37%, while the older group's rate climbed to 78%, expanding the divide from 12 to 41 percentage points.

But the decline in young homeownership may reflect something besides worsening affordability: Denver's success in attracting young workers.

"Two things are likely at work. One is the affordability decline itself. The other is Denver’s growth as an economic hub that appeals to young workers, many of whom arrive as renters," says Jones. "That adds renters to the mix and dilutes the young homeownership rate, even for people who never intended to buy."

There, younger households were already far less likely to own homes in 1980, when their homeownership rate stood at 28%. By 2024, it had slipped only slightly, to 26%.

Older New Yorkers, meanwhile, saw their homeownership rate climb from approximately 43% to 63% over the same period.

"In New York, homeownership has always been expensive and out of reach for most young households, so there was little room to fall," Jones explains. "Young homeownership slipped only slightly, which suggests the current rate is close to a floor."

She suggests low COVID-19 pandemic-era mortgage rates may have helped some older households that had been waiting to purchase finally enter the market.

And regardless of how the divide developed, entering homeownership later can carry lasting financial consequences.

Separate research from Realtor.com, co-authored by Jones, found that purchasing a home by age 30 was associated with 22.5% higher net worth—approximately $119,000 more—by age 50, compared with buying in one's 40s, even after accounting for income, education, and marital status.

Those advantages can extend across generations, too. Children raised in homeowner households were 18.4 percentage points more likely to become homeowners themselves by age 35, the same research found.

One of the Urban Institute's most striking findings concerns a milestone that comes before homeownership: establishing an independent household.

In 1980, young adults in high-cost metropolitan areas were slightly more likely than their counterparts nationally to head their own households. By 2024, that relationship had reversed.

Just 41% of young adults in expensive markets were household heads, the lowest share among the study's housing cost categories.

Instead, more are living with parents, other relatives, or roommates. Research from Realtor.com backs this up, finding that a third of young adults lived with their parents across the country in 2025.

Yet expensive cities haven't lost their appeal. The share of young households living in high-cost markets actually edged up from 28% in 1980 to 31% in 2024, partly reflecting a broader shift toward urban areas.

What's changed is their housing tenure. In those markets, the homeownership rate among younger households fell from 40% to 32% over the same period.

So young adults are continuing to pursue opportunities in expensive cities, but fewer are establishing households of their own once they get there. And another finding suggests that rapidly rising prices may be changing the age composition of metropolitan areas, regardless of how expensive those places were to begin with.

Between 2014 and 2024, metropolitan areas experiencing faster home price appreciation generally saw declines in young adults' share of the population, the Urban Institute found.

The relationship held across high-, moderate-, and low-cost markets. But Jones cautions that the findings don't necessarily mean young people are being priced out.

"That can come from young people leaving, older people moving in, or both," she says. "Florida metros on the included chart may be an example. Their older populations are large and grew significantly during the pandemic, which could erode the young share on its own."

Indeed, the relationship between home prices and demographic changes could run in either direction.

"Young people may be fleeing places where costs are climbing, or older, more financially equipped buyers may be moving in and competing for homes," Jones says. "That pushes prices up, and the newcomers then make up a larger share of the population."

Determining whether younger residents are actually leaving would require examining changes in the number of young adults, not just their share of the population.

Still, other economic research suggests that housing costs can constrain where workers pursue employment.

A May 2025 analysis from the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond found that geographic mobility has declined across all age groups since the 1990s. Among the contributing factors, researchers identified restrictions on housing supply in economically productive cities, where high costs can discourage workers from relocating to pursue better opportunities.

The researchers also identified another potential obstacle: Older homeowners have become less responsive to rising local housing costs, making them more likely to stay put even as prices climb. In supply-constrained markets, that can make it harder for newcomers to move in.

Meanwhile, a February 2026 analysis from the St. Louis Fed found that home prices had risen approximately 207% from 2000 to 2024, outpacing the roughly 155% increase in per-capita incomes.

Together, the findings suggest that the costs of entering high-opportunity housing markets could affect younger Americans' earnings prospects as well as their ability to build wealth.

There may be a way around that trade-off for some.

"Remote work may be loosening the link between where people live and where the jobs are, which could enable more households to achieve homeownership without giving up job opportunities," Jones says.

But that flexibility is not available to everyone. Workers whose jobs require them to be physically present may face a more difficult choice between buying a home where they can afford one and pursuing careers in the cities where their skills command the highest wages.

And unlike the wealth accumulated by longtime homeowners, the career opportunities they pass up may be difficult to recover later.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

— "Things went even better than expected," said Shaughnessy Naughton, the group's founder

The midterm results earlier this month included the election of several physicians and other healthcare professionals to federal and statewide seats, especially on the Democratic side. MedPage Today Washington Editor Joyce Frieden spoke with Shaughnessy Naughton, founder and president of 314 Action, about the organization's role in helping to get some of these clinicians -- as well as scientists -- elected to office. The conversation, which was conducted over the phone with a public relations person present, has been edited for length and clarity.

How did your organization do in terms of seeing its chosen candidates elected?

Things went even better than expected. We are the only organization to elect Democratic scientists and doctors to all levels of government -- 14 members to the House, including 10 who took seats from Republicans -- two new doctors to the Senate, which hasn't had Democratic doctors serving in close to 60 years; and a Democratic doctor as governor in Ohio, the first woman doctor-governor in the country.

There's a couple of arms to that answer. First, we recruited and invested early in quality candidates. Additionally, this was a healthcare election and our candidates leaned into their backgrounds as doctors and as problem-solvers to present a clear contrast with their opponents that have overseen, particularly in the federal races, the slashing of Medicaid, the elimination of the [Affordable Care Act Enhanced Premium Tax Credit], the assault on rural health, and on and on.

Then you couple that with [HHS Secretary] Robert F. Kennedy Jr. -- the vaccine delusionist -- overseeing HHS during one health crisis after another, leading to preventable deaths from measles and preventable diseases. So I think all of that compounded to really create a lane that voters saw as a viable and important alternative to what they currently had.

Annie Andrews, MD, [D-S.C. senator-elect] is at the top of that list. South Carolina hasn't elected a Democrat statewide, I think, in over 20 years. It is very hard to change people's voting patterns, but it does speak to the strength of her message and her candidacy that she was able to not only get elected, but she brought along a congressional race in South Carolina -- one that flipped to Democrat -- and 10 statehouse seats. Wow!

We are really looking forward to what she can accomplish in the Senate. I was having coffee this morning with a senator who had just met her at orientation this week, and he said he told her to "Lean in and make sure your voice is being heard because we really need you right now." I think that that is true coming from the senator's mouth, but I think it's also true coming from the voters' mouth.

You mentioned the vaccine issue and the Affordable Care Act tax credits. What other healthcare issues are you hoping to see acted on in the new Congress?

We were promised [by the current administration and Congress] to see a reduction in healthcare costs, and we've seen the exact opposite. Premiums continue to skyrocket. Out-of-pocket costs and deductibles just keep going up, and there doesn't seem to be much relief on prescription drug prices either.

This is at a time when we're having record numbers of foodborne illness outbreaks and measles deaths and spread. The threshold for herd immunity is 95% for measles, and most kindergarteners' classes are below that at this point. So it really does call to have strong health leaders leading with facts and evidence and their values to protect Americans' health and make healthcare more affordable.

We are looking for action on healthcare affordability and accessibility, and holding the administration accountable for what, to say the least, have been questionable choices such as the approval of candy-flavored vapes, so we do expect that Congress should be able to deliver on both.

Even though they don't have enough votes to override a presidential veto?

What happens remains to be seen. The moves from the administration do not [suggest] that they want to work with Democrats, but the remaining Republicans in the House still have elections in 2 years, and the American people spoke loud and clear that they want relief from high prices across the board.

Can you explain more about your organization's role? I understand you spent more than $30 million this cycle. Do you recruit as well as contribute financially?

Yes, we are involved in recruiting. One of the things we're seeing bearing fruit is an investment at the state and local level. One of the people we endorsed in the 2018 cycle was [microbiologist] Jasmine Clark, PhD. She ran in a Republican district in the Georgia statehouse and flipped the seat. This year she stepped up to run for a congressional seat, and won.

We work with campaigns, helping them put together their campaign strategy, a financing plan, and consulting teams. We find staff and work at the grassroots level with them. Often our campaign staff will be in the district with them when they launch, and our communications staff works with them on media training.

We have individual donors; this cycle we had 150,000 individual contributors. Their first donation average is $10; the lifetime average is $17. People usually donate three times a year and many have been donating to us for 3, 4, or 5 years. We do a lot of grassroots fundraising, and we also have been the beneficiary of [former New York City Mayor] Michael Bloomberg's generosity this cycle, which makes a lot of sense because he is someone invested in public health and public health education.

We have candidates fill out a questionnaire, which is on our website. And we are already thinking about 2028 -- even 2027 has some local elections [of interest]. We need to play everywhere. When you run credible candidates, they can resonate and make a difference and get elected.

What is your background and how did you end up starting 314 Action?

I was a chemist and worked in breast cancer research and drug discovery, and I worked on creating an antibiotic to combat superbugs. In 2014, I became concerned by the antiscience rhetoric coming out of so many politicians, so I decided to run for Congress in Bucks County, Pennsylvania, where I'm from. But I didn't have 314 Action and was locked out of the [standard] donor network, so I started cold-calling chemists and making my case and building out a network from there.

Ultimately, I didn't win, but I learned a lot in the process and part of what I learned is that it's very hard to break into politics when you don't have that traditional political background. And so I founded 314 Action to break down those barriers, to recruit, train, and elect people with scientific backgrounds, with the thinking that there isn't an issue that doesn't benefit by having data-driven analytical thinkers actually at the governing table.

#5611. Most nonprofit hospitals' tax breaks outpaced their community spending in 2023: Lown Institute

Most nonprofit hospitals' tax breaks outpaced their community spending in 2023: Lown Institute" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Just over half of the country’s nonprofit hospitals have charity care and community benefit investments that fall short of their tax savings, according to the latest of the Lown Institute’s analyses on more than 3,000 hospitals’ tax filings.

In 2023, the most recent year in which Internal Revenue Service Form 990s were available for review, the think tank identified $38.8 billion of industry-wide tax exemptions, or $12.8 million per hospital and 3.8% of total expenses on average. About $37.1 billion was collectively spent by the same hospitals on various community benefits, as reported in the IRS forms matched to other filings such as Medicare cost reports.

While the total exemption handily outpaces the benefits investments by Lown’s measure, the group underscored that these "fair share” deficits or surpluses also vary widely between facilities, and that some of the industry’s biggest names are on the wrong side of the divide.

Here, Mayo Clinic Hospital led the pack with a $366 million deficit, according to Lown’s analysis, followed by Tisch Hospital (-$294 million deficit), Stanford Hospital (-$255 million deficit), New York-Presbyterian Hospital (-$248 million deficit) and Massachusetts General Hospital (-$219 million deficit).

"Some of America's wealthiest hospitals fall hundreds of millions short of giving back what they receive from their communities, leaving those with fewer resources to pick up the slack," Vikas Saini, M.D., president of the Lown Institute, said in a release on the new analysis, released Tuesday.

Among those leading the latter group were North Shore University Hospital ($167 fair share surplus), Rochester General Hospital ($146 million surplus) and Englewood Hospital ($142 million surplus). Lown’s analysis includes a searchable hospital-by-hospital breakdown of the tax exemptions and community investment totals.

When splitting the 52% of deficit hospitals apart from the surplus hospitals, the former group logged about $15.5 billion above their reported community benefits—a deficit Lown said could wipe the medical debt of 12 million Americans. Fair share surplus hospitals outpaced their exemptions by $13.8 billion.

Total tax exemptions were also “very unevenly distributed” among the hospitals, Lown said. The 30 hospitals, or about 1% of all hospitals, with the largest tax exemptions collectively avoided $6.8 billion, or about 18% of total exemptions. The 607 hospitals, or about 20%, accounted for three-quarters of the country’s hospital tax exemptions.

Lown’s measure of nonprofit hospitals’ tax breaks includes exemptions from federal and state corporate income taxes, state and local sales taxes, property taxes, tax-exempt bonds, tax-exempt charitable donations and federal unemployment tax exemptions. Not included are other benefits provided to many nonprofits, like Medicaid disproportionate share payments, 340B discounts or profits from indirect tax arbitrage.

Its tally of community benefit includes spending on patient financial assistance, subsidized care, payments to other nonprofits to improve health or various community health or social determinants of health investments.

Of note, it excludes Medicaid shortfall—the difference between hospitals’ costs and revenues when treating Medicaid patients—and spending on professional education and research. The hospital industry typically points to these billions of dollars of exclusions when discussing their tax breaks, with Medicaid shortfall alone accounting for nearly half of their preferred community benefit spending totals. Lown noted in its methodology that these accounting losses are often offset by other discounts and supplemental benefits and don’t always have a direct impact on community health, among other objections.

Lown said the disparities between hospitals and the outsized benefits being delivered by some are a call to amend, not eliminate, nonprofit status exemptions. The think tank accompanied its analysis with calls to increase reporting transparency and set spending targets for hospitals tied to variables such as size, exemption value, financial health and prior spending.

“Tax exemptions aren't a gift—they're an expectation, and regulators need to make sure all hospitals hold up their end of the bargain," Saini said.

Lown acknowledged the impending financial pressure hospitals will face with upcoming H.R. 1 policy changes and said such changes should be accompanied by “short-term” financial protections.

Still, the group isn’t alone in drawing scrutiny to the tax breaks. Lawmakers and policy advisors have pointed to, and questioned the justification for, nonprofits’ exemptions when questioning health system leaders on collections policies or high prices.

Academics and researchers have also called for greater transparency or other overhauls of how community benefits are reported or calculated. Of note, a research article published earlier this month in Health Affairs reviewing hospital filings between 2013 and 2022 outlined a disconnect between different hospitals’ listed charity care eligibility thresholds and their relative spending, which more closely aligned with community need than their stated policy.

#5609. FDA Adds Another Player in ALK-Positive Lung Cancer

— Among the indications, neladalkib approved in second-line after alectinib

The FDA granted accelerated approval to the third-generation ALK inhibitor neladalkib (Nelkarmi) for previously treated advanced ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), making it the seventh approved agent in a crowded therapeutic field.

The approval limits use to patients with unresectable locally advanced or metastatic ALK-positive NSCLC previously treated with alectinib (Alecensa) or at least two prior ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors and platinum-based chemotherapy.

Support for the conditional approval came from 222 patients in the phase I/II single-arm ALKOVE-1 trial.

In the cohort of 67 patients who had only received alectinib in the metastatic setting, neladalkib induced responses in 49%, with a duration of response (DOR) of at least 6 months in 76% of the responding patients. For the cohort of 155 patients previously treated with two or more ALK inhibitors and platinum-based chemotherapy, 32% responded, with a DOR of at least 6 months for 69% of the responders. The proportion of responders with DORs of at least 12 months was 52% and 51% for the two cohorts, respectively.

"Patients with ALK-positive lung cancer are often treated with multiple targeted therapies over many years," said investigator Alice Shaw, MD, PhD, of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston, in a press release from drugmaker GSK. "Advances in treatment have brought us closer to the goal of managing ALK-positive lung cancer as a chronic condition, but balancing disease control and long-term tolerability remains a significant challenge. The approval of neladalkib provides an important new treatment option for patients."

An analysis reported at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) meeting showed a response rate of 26% among patients with exposure to lorlatinib (Lorbrena), the only other approved third-generation ALK inhibitor, versus 46% in patients not previously treated with lorlatinib. DORs of at least 6 or 12 months in the lorlatinib-treated subgroup occurred in 68% and 54% of responders.

In the full cohort of patients presented at the meeting (median three prior lines of therapy), landmark analyses of progression-free survival (PFS) showed a 6-month PFS of 50%, 12-month PFS of 33%, and 18-month PFS of 28% for patients treated with neladalkib. Median PFS was 5.7 months, increasing to 14.5 months in patients not previously treated with lorlatinib. Additionally, a third of patients with brain metastases had objective responses with neladalkib.

At the ASCO meeting, invited discussant Angel Qin, MD, of the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, said the ALKOVE-1 results suggest neladalkib has potential as an option in the post-lorlatinib setting, albeit with relatively modest activity, and a manageable side-effect profile.

The most common adverse events (AEs) were elevated liver enzymes, which occurred in almost half of patients and was grade ≥3 severity in 15-20% of patients. Other AEs occurring in at least 20% of patients were musculoskeletal pain, constipation, dysgeusia, peripheral neuropathy, edema, and fatigue. Prescribing information for neladalkib includes warnings and precautions for hepatotoxicity, renal toxicity, ocular toxicity, creatine phosphokinase elevation, and embryo-fetal toxicity.

The ongoing phase III ALKAZAR trial of neladalkib in the first-line setting may provide more information about the drug's potential as upfront therapy in advanced ALK-positive NSCLC. A preliminary analysis from ALKOVE-1 at ASCO showed an objective response rate of 86% for patients with no prior ALK-targeted therapy.

HHS finalizes updates to HIPAA privacy rule to ease patient access to health information" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The final rule, issued by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights (OCR), strengthens and clarifies the right of an individual to access their protected health information and reduces regulatory and administrative burdens, the agency said.

The proposed rule was issued more than five years ago, in January 2021. An unpublished version of the final rule is available here.

Under the final rule, healthcare organizations must respond faster to patient requests for copies of their health records. HHS said covered entities will have no more than 15 calendar days to respond to a request, reduced from the current 30-day period. Organizations are allowed one extension of no more than 30 calendar days, HHS said in the final rule.

The rule also establishes that patients can access their protected health information through personal health apps when the covered entity has the technical capacity to deliver the records in that form and format.

The rule also expands circumstances when patients must receive copies of their health records for free, requires advance notice of fees and modifies identity verification requirements.

To make it easier for healthcare organizations to share data for care coordination, the final rule clarifies that health plans may use and disclose protected health information for care coordination and case management for individuals. The rule also expressly permits covered entities to disclose PHI to social services agencies, community-based organizations and similar third parties for care coordination and case management for individuals.

“Americans should never have to fight for access to their own health records,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr in a statement. “Under President Trump’s leadership, we are putting patients in control, requiring faster access to their information, and cutting red tape that gets in the way of coordinated care. This rule modernizes HIPAA to serve patients and help providers spend more time delivering care and less time navigating bureaucracy.”

Provisions in the final rule will become effective 60 days after publication in the Federal Register, and compliance will be required 180 days after that date, according to HHS in a fact sheet.

Gleason said there are three main components of the rule: the designation of a "personal health app," identity verification and speed. "It should be almost instantaneous with electronic data, and it also says that this information is free to the patient," she said.

“This final rule provides Americans with faster and easier access to their health information, which is critical to them being able to take control of their own health and health care,” said Office for Civil Rights Director Paula M. #5607. Can America Build More Housing Without Gutting Historic Protections? Inside the Senate’s Permitting Battle

A sweeping permitting reform package moved closer to a final Senate vote Monday, when lawmakers voted 70–27 to limit debate on legislation that could weaken a federal safeguard for historic places.

At issue is Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which requires federal agencies to consider how projects they fund, approve, or permit might affect historic properties—and consult with those affected before proceeding.

The proposed changes would exempt most projects whose only federal connection is financial assistance, while imposing tighter deadlines and restricting legal challenges.

As the nation confronts a shortage of 4.03 million homes and an aging energy grid, supporters argue that reducing regulatory hurdles will accelerate infrastructure development. But preservation advocates warn the changes could leave communities with less influence over what gets built—and what gets lost.

"Preservation is not a hindrance to progress," Heather Veneziano, director of Tulane University's Historic Preservation Program, told Realtor.com® during a recent walking interview through Bayou St. John, one of New Orleans' oldest neighborhoods.

Rather than keeping neighborhoods frozen in time, she argued, preservation can help communities determine how they evolve.

"Keeping things static is impossible," Veneziano said.

New Orleans provides a particularly salient standpoint from which to understand Veneziano’s perspective.

The city is home to 26 nationally recognized historic districts encompassing more than 45,000 properties and roughly 40% of its urbanized area, according to the city. Indeed, its architectural heritage is so extensive that it became the only entire city included on the World Monuments Fund's Irreplaceable America list.

Veneziano helped lead the nomination, informed in part by the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina and the connections to place that could not be rebuilt elsewhere.

"You lose all your really strong ties and connections to place, but also to people," she said of the communities uprooted after the devastating 2005 superstorm. "And places don't matter without people."

But Veneziano sees the buildings themselves as part of what makes those communities viable.

"It's an economic driver for the community, it's housing at a basic level for the community," she said. "Those are the containers for all of the services that happen in your community."

Along Bayou St. John, Veneziano pointed to the Pitot House, built in 1799, as an example of another kind of value older buildings retain.

Its elevated living quarters reflect a time when residents built knowing water would eventually come, while its surviving materials offer lessons in constructing homes suited to Louisiana's flood risks.

Yet, those lessons might have been erased had preservationists not found a way to accommodate another pressing community need.

In 1964, the religious order that owned the property needed land for a girls' school. Rather than allow its demolition, preservationists raised money to move the house 220 feet down the street on flatbed trucks.

The compromise allowed both the school and the house to continue serving the community. And today, the deal serves as a reminder of how preservation can accommodate development rather than prevent it.

Not every historic property can be relocated, however, and the expense of finding alternatives can test even the most committed to protecting a neighborhood's housing resources.

In March, Jane Place Neighborhood Sustainability Initiative, a community land trust dedicated to permanently affordable housing, sought permission to demolish a century-old shotgun house in Mid-City.

The nonprofit argued that rehabilitation would be prohibitively expensive and higher-density construction would better serve the property.

Preservation authorities disagreed, finding insufficient evidence that the house was beyond repair. Jane Place eventually withdrew its appeal without a finalized replacement development plan.

The spat concerned local demolition rules, not Section 106. But it exposed competing interpretations of how best to protect a neighborhood's housing resources: Preserve an existing home or make room for more?

Veneziano acknowledged that unclear local requirements can frustrate homeowners trying to maintain or renovate their properties.

"If your municipality doesn't have their act together and isn't clear about what their guidelines are," she said, "it can be very challenging to homeowners."

In a city facing an estimated shortage of 44,000 affordable rental units, the case for preserving old buildings can be difficult to reconcile with the urgent need for new homes. But elsewhere in the Big Easy, a long-vacant public building offers another approach.

In September, a century-old firehouse reopened after decades of vacancy, transformed into seven affordable apartments above an early-childhood education center.

The mixed-use redevelopment cost approximately $8 million, including $1.35 million in state historic tax credits and $725,000 in federal disaster recovery funds.

"The Louisiana Avenue Firehouse shows us that demolition of historic buildings is not always the answer," Louisiana Housing Corporation Executive Director Kevin Delahoussaye said.

But the very public investment that helped save the building also triggered Section 106 review—and that additional requirement is what housing advocates argue can make federally assisted developments more expensive and difficult to finance.

Their argument is simple: More reviews take more time. More time costs more money. And combined, that can make a project not worth it.

YIMBY Action, which supports the proposed Section 106 exemption, estimates that at least $10 billion annually in federal housing and community development funding could move faster under the broader permitting package, citing delays that can jeopardize financing or discourage developers from accepting public money altogether.

Veneziano emphasized that preservationists aren't simply trying to "save this fancy house." Their work, she explained, is "really community engagement"—helping residents recognize and protect histories that might otherwise be overlooked.

That concern brought hundreds of preservationists, civil rights advocates, and tribal representatives to the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 9 to oppose changes to Section 106.

"Our sacred places are living places of prayer," Harry Antonio Jr., governor of the Pueblo of Laguna in New Mexico, told the crowd.

The Senate proposal would narrow consideration of certain effects on historic places, including noise and visual impacts, raising concerns about the protection of sacred landscapes, burial grounds, and other culturally significant sites.

Veneziano pointed to a conflict farther upriver in Wallace, LA, where federal scrutiny exposed problems with a developer's assessment of a proposed grain terminal.

There, descendants of enslaved residents opposed the project, which would have been built near historic plantations, burial grounds, and their predominantly Black community.

A ProPublica investigation revealed that an archaeological consultant's original findings about potential harm to historic sites had been stripped from a report prepared for the developer. The Army Corps of Engineers subsequently rejected the assessment as insufficient and demanded further investigation.

In April 2024, the Corps determined that noise, light pollution, and the terminal's industrial appearance would adversely affect Wallace's historic character—precisely the kinds of impacts the Senate proposal would subject to a narrower standard of review.

The company behind the terminal abandoned the project later that year, blaming prolonged permitting delays. Residents celebrated the outcome as a victory.

Such lengthy reviews, however, may be the exception rather than the rule.

An October analysis by Virginia's Department of Historic Resources found that 85% of nearly 9,900 projects completed Section 106 review within 30 days. Just 6% took longer than 90 days, primarily because they required additional surveys or involved potential harm to historic properties.

Those figures aren't necessarily representative nationwide, nor do they establish whether reviews actually delayed construction.

"If you're trying to get a project through, yeah, it's annoying," Veneziano acknowledged.

Still, Section 106 doesn't prohibit development. It requires agencies to consider the consequences and potential alternatives before proceeding.

And as Congress weighs how to accelerate construction, lawmakers will also confront a more fundamental question: Who gets to determine what a community can afford to lose?

Veneziano posed a question of her own: "How do we take the best of what we have, and build upon it into the future?"

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5606. HLTH 2026: GLP-1 costs remain a challenge. A new CVS study aims to identify the right price

HLTH 2026: GLP-1 costs remain a challenge. A new CVS study aims to identify the right price" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Cost and access to GLP-1s remains a challenge, but the benefits of these drugs aren't in doubt.

A new study from CVS Health aims to quantify at what price a GLP-1 drug has generated enough savings elsewhere through improved clinical outcomes. The healthcare giant used anonymized claims data from Aetna members in fully insured plans and found savings from reduced hospital and medical spending, as well as improved health outcomes.

But those benefits weren't enough to offset the increased pharmaceutical spending at the current price point, the study found.

The study tracked a mix of members who took GLP-1s from 2023 to 2025, so some patients had three years of follow-up care and management.

Amy Compton-Phillips, M.D., chief medical officer at CVS, told Fierce Healthcare that part of the challenge in this equation is that these drugs gained steam as a treatment for obesity at a high price. And while those costs have come down, the reductions haven't yet been enough to offset the expenditures.

Another challenge for employers in particular—where GLP-1 coverage has been most in flux—is turnover, she said. While GLP-1s do drive significant improvements, an employer may not reap the benefit of the reduced cost if an employee moves to a different company before those are realized, even though they paid for the medication initially.

The study sought to identify a price point where those savings would be felt and landed at $350 per month over a three-year period. Achieving that, Compton-Phillips said, would likely lure employers into embracing broader GLP-1 coverage.

"For them, it might be really worthwhile to say, 'Hey, at this price point, I can afford to cover this for my employees, knowing that in the near term the savings will pay for my investment,'" she said.

The study found obesity rates declining after a 2022 peak, as well as a reduction of between 34% and 42% in hospitalizations over three years. Patients also had 14% lower odds of a serious cardiac event.

For patients who remained on the drugs for three years, their total medical spending decreased by $9,400, but associated pharmacy spending increased in tandem by $13,300, the study found.

Clinical improvements also fell off when patients were not able to remain adherent to the medication over several years, highlighting the importance of a wraparound approach that supports broader care management rather than simply prescribing a patient a GLP-1.

Compton-Phillips said CVS' own weight management program brings nutrition, peer coaching and other supports into the fold, in addition to the prescription. This is especially critical, she said, as evidence suggests weight gain is common after a patient stops taking their GLP-1, making behavior change key.

"At the moment, there's not great evidence that if you come off the drugs, you will maintain the weight loss," she said.

The CVS researchers said that the ultimate goal of the study was not to demand that all GLP-1 prescriptions repay their own costs, but to ensure that drug costs align with patient benefits and the broader cost of access. By lowering the net price of these products, more people can access them, the study concludes.

"These drugs make people's lives better, and I want to give them out," Compton-Phillips said. Doing so becomes a challenge, though, "at the price they are today," she said.
