#5605. Erectile Dysfunction Drug Shows Mixed Results in Alzheimer's

— AR1001 missed the primary endpoint in one population, but slowed decline in another

Mirodenafil (known as AR1001), an oral phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor approved in South Korea to treat erectile dysfunction, showed mixed results in people with early Alzheimer's disease in the phase III POLARIS-AD trial.

The treatment missed the primary endpoint in one prespecified group but showed positive results in another, reported Sharon Sha, MD, MS, of Stanford University in Palo Alto, California, at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease conference in Boston.

In the overall study population, AR1001 showed a nonsignificant difference of -0.11 points versus placebo in Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) scores at 52 weeks (P=0.4015). CDR-SB scores measure cognitive and functional impairment and can range from 0 to 18.

In a population of monotherapy patients -- those not on an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor or memantine at baseline -- AR1001 demonstrated a significant 52-week treatment difference of -0.44 points versus placebo (P=0.0266), representing a 31% slowing of decline.

Secondary endpoints of cognitive and functional measures trended in favor of AR1001 in both populations, with a nominally significant difference in Mini-Mental State Examination scores emerging in the monotherapy population.

The most frequent adverse events were diarrhea, falls, and dizziness. Adverse events led to discontinuation in 5.2% of patients in the AR1001 group and 1.7% in the placebo group.

Serious adverse events were similar in the AR1001 group (10.0%) and the placebo group (9.8%). Four deaths occurred in the AR1001 group (acute myeloid leukemia, cerebrovascular accident, suicide, and ruptured cerebral aneurysm) and three deaths occurred in the placebo group.

The CDR-SB data and safety profile are encouraging, Sha noted. "POLARIS-AD made its primary efficacy endpoint in the prespecified monotherapy population," she said. "The secondary endpoints had trends in favor of AR1001."

AR1001 is a brain-penetrant phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor that enhances cyclic guanosine monophosphate (GMP) signaling. In preclinical Alzheimer's models, the treatment improved cognitive performance and reduced amyloid and tau burdens.

"AR1001 takes a novel approach, relaxing blood vessels to increase blood flow to the brain," noted Richard Oakley, PhD, of the Alzheimer's Society in England, who wasn't involved in the study.

"AR1001 is from the same family of medicines as Viagra [sildenafil], but it is being developed specifically for Alzheimer's disease. People should not take Viagra to try to treat Alzheimer's," Oakley said in a statement. "We look forward to seeing the full results from this trial and how this drug progresses."

In 2024, a study of 270,000 men in the U.K. linked erectile dysfunction drugs with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's disease. Those findings conflicted with data from the NIH DREAM initiative, but supported an earlier study of Medicare beneficiaries that suggested that sildenafil users were less likely to develop Alzheimer's than non-users.

The POLARIS-AD trial included 1,535 amyloid-positive Alzheimer's patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia in the overall population; the monotherapy subgroup had 604 patients. The average patient age in the study was 73, and just over half were women. Participants were randomized to receive AR1001 30 mg or placebo once daily for 52 weeks.

The primary endpoint was the 52-week change in CDR-SB score in the overall and monotherapy populations. The primary efficacy objective required a significant treatment difference compared with placebo at week 52 in at least one population under the prespecified multiplicity procedure. The prespecified plan was suggested by AR1001's phase II findings, Sha pointed out.

Biomarker tests showed that AR1001 increased cyclic GMP levels in cerebrospinal fluid compared with placebo at week 52 in both the overall (P<0.0001) and monotherapy populations (P=0.0058), supporting target engagement, Sha said.

The presentation included no data about sex differences in treatment effects and Sha said the company has not yet run those analyses. "These results are hot off the press as of Friday," she noted, adding that "continuing analysis is happening, and the open-label extension is ongoing."

#5603. Builders Are Slashing Mortgage Rates To Win Buyers, but Hold Firm on Sticker Prices

Prices for new homes have been stagnant for years. That leaves room for potential homebuyers if they're on the hunt for good incentives.

The latest Realtor.com® quarterly construction insights report shows that prices on new homes are holding steady, but builders are having to get creative to attract buyers, relying on rate buydowns and other incentives as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate stays above 7%.

The median listing price for new builds hit $451,071 in the third quarter. It's been right around that number since late 2023. Builders are starting fewer homes in the inflation-plagued economy.

Increased labor and material costs and decreased buyer demand led to the completion rate of new single-family homes falling 11.0% year over year in September.

Meanwhile, existing-home prices came in 1.5% below 2025 levels, landing at $402,883. New homes have to compete with existing homes for buyers, and the rise in existing-home sales shows that some cost-conscious buyers who might have built new are choosing existing, instead. Existing-home sales just hit a 16-year low.

"Builders were quicker to adjust to the realities of muted buyer demand in this high-rate environment, while existing-home sellers had pricing expectations based on the market from 2021 and 2022 that were slower to dissolve," Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner writes in the report. "The overall price softness we’ve seen through 2026 is driven primarily by the existing-home segment."

That's led to more builders and sellers tempering their expectations. Resellers cut prices on 21.6% of homes this quarter. Builders are doing the same for 20.9% of their stock.

"The growing incidence of price reductions for new and existing homes is an indication of softness in the housing market in general and gives reason to expect that the diminished pace of inventory growth will continue," writes Berner.

Homebuilders this year are reporting that the difficult housing market is eating into margins. Some have retooled to the higher end of the market, which is less affected by affordability concerns. Others have dangled more incentives to bring buyers calling.

That's led to some oddities, and it means the market for new homes is, in a lot of ways, buyer-friendly.

For instance, existing homes are more expensive than new ones based on the price per square foot: $218 for new homes, $219 for existing ones. That's because, while there's a $50,000 gap between the median new-home price and the median existing-home price, new homes are bigger: a median of 2,056 square feet compared to 1,790 square feet. So, adjusting for size, this price gap disappears.

Also, new builds are concentrated in the South, where land is cheaper. Existing-home sales in the much more expensive Northeast, meanwhile, drives up the data. So, nationally, the median sales price for new homes was $400,400 while for existing homes it was $417,500.

For builders, reduced rates are the most common type of buyer incentive, helping homebuyers cut down on the total cost of ownership. This quarter, the average starting mortgage rate for new-home buyers was 5.01%. For existing-home buyers, it was 6.15%.

"In today’s environment of higher-for-longer mortgage rates, this is an enticing marketing strategy. Builders often have strong relationships with mortgage lenders to whom they send lots of their buyers, and in exchange for this volume of loan origination, the lenders can offer below-market rates."

But the savings aren't always permanent. But even with temporary benefits, like the popular 3/2/1 step-down, buyers still see a big benefit in cost savings.

With inflation high and mortgage rates elevated, what's going to break the cycle?

The housing market over the next year will remain challenged, Goldman Sachs said in its latest forecast. It predicts home prices will keep growing at an "anemic" 1% in 2027.

“In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity,” economists Ronnie Walker and David Mericle wrote. “The combination of mortgage borrowers refinancing at low rates en masse in 2020 and 2021 and the high current level of mortgage rates has created a significant financial cost to moving."

If mortgage rates do start to come down next year, that could bring buyers off the sidelines and cause housing activity to pick up. Goldman projected that could be the case in late 2027.

Some areas are more immune. Maor Greenberg, co-founder and CEO of structural engineer Spacial, says builders feel squeezed by rate hikes, as carrying costs go up on houses that are already under construction. Then, the buyer deals with a higher mortgage rate. The higher end of the market and booming areas like the tech-awash San Francisco Bay Area are rare exceptions.

"Even in a soft market, there’s a point where starting to build a house makes more sense than waiting for more favorable conditions, because you’re paying money to hold on to land," Greenberg says. "That moves the problem down to selling: To do that, builders offer incentives and cut prices. Margins get tighter, but you’re not losing as much money.”

Ryan Serhant, speaking exclusively to Realtor.com, recently offered his own advice on the market: Don't wait for lower rates.

While it might seem like the housing market will stay frozen forever, there are some cities where buyers can get a good deal. And a whole lot of other people are thinking the same thing.

“Everyone wants low rates, they never want what comes with it," he said. "You know what'll happen if rates come down? There will be no houses for sale.”

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5602. Humana launches national provider Gold Card program

Humana launches national provider Gold Card program" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Humana is continuing its push to reform prior authorization with the launch of a national provider gold card program.

The program will go into effect on Dec. 1, the company announced Tuesday. It will focus initially on MRI, CT and MRA imaging as well as physical and occupational therapy. Through the program, eligible providers will no longer need to secure a prior authorization approval and can instead use a streamlined process.

Humana estimates that about 50,000 providers will qualify for the program. Eligible providers must be able to demonstrate a proven track record of high-quality care and patient outcomes.

Traci Granston, M.D., vice president of clinical innovation and trend at Humana, told Fierce Healthcare in an exclusive interview that prior authorization and other utilization management approaches are key in ensuring that patients receive the appropriate care.

However, lengthy decision times and other barriers can create a painful friction. So for providers that consistently demonstrate that they are aligned with clinical guidelines, the gold cards can remove that guardrail.

"If they're following those guidelines and providing appropriate care, prior auths don't really serve a purpose for them," Granston said.

The insurer conducted a pilot earlier this year with about 400 provider organizations and approximately 8,000 clinicians. Through that process, the team conducted interviews with clinicians and office staff who shared their desire for fewer administrative burdens and a simpler experience.

Those insights shaped the broader launch, Humana said, and the insurer intends to continue to iterate and evolve the gold card program over time, including by adding new service lines. It's not uncommon for a program to roll out that aims to support providers, but their voice is less often at the table in shaping what the experience looks like to ensure that their pain points are being addressed.

Granston said that the team is examining more time-sensitive services that could fit within the program, for example.

"For our top-performing providers, we would like to essentially get out of the way and let them continue to care for our members," she said.

The gold card program builds on Humana's existing work to reform prior authorization, including a streamlined approval process for electronic submissions that took effect in January of this year. Under this initiative, Humana responds within one business day in 95% of electronic prior authorization cases.

The insurer also announced earlier this month that it would join forces with athenahealth to accelerate the use of electronic prior authorization. Through the partnership, more of the process is embedded directly in the provider's workflow, streamlining the experience for them at the point of care.

Granston said that the goal is to make it easier to surface the data necessary to make an approval and enable that to occur in real time. This also means that fewer people have to be dedicated to the work of submissions and approval.

"When the information exists, you don't really need all these people to be touching it," she said.

#5601. Macrotroponins One Reason Not to Take cTnI Readings at Face Value

— High cTnI less of a red flag when macro-cTnI is also in the picture

Beware attempts to interpret cardiac troponin (cTn) as a cardiovascular risk marker without accounting for the presence of macrotroponins, researchers warned.

In a cohort study of community dwellers in Norway, high cardiac troponin I (cTnI; >10 ng/L) without any macro-cTnI was associated with a whopping 50.0% rate of incident cardiovascular events over a median follow-up of 8.3 years, according to a group led by Torbjørn Omland, MD, MPH, of University of Oslo and Akershus University Hospital in Lørenskog, Norway.

This was a significant jump in cardiovascular risk compared to those with high cTnI and prevalent macro-cTnI (6.8%; adjusted HR 8.5, 95% CI 3.1-23.6) or those whose cTnI readings were deemed too low to merit additional macro-cTnI testing (7.2% in the group with cTnI <5 ng/L; adjusted HR 6.1, 95% CI 3.2-11.6).

"The salient novel findings of the current population-based study are that macro-cTnI is highly prevalent in individuals in the general population with cTnI >10 ng/L by the widely used Abbott high-sensitivity assay and that macrotroponin presence may obscure the true association between cTnI and the incidence of cardiovascular events," Omland and colleagues reported in European Heart Journal.

Macrotroponins are high-molecular-weight complexes formed by cTn autoantibodies and circulating cTn molecules. These large complexes are slower to clear than cTn alone, which can cause assays to read higher.

With macrotroponin I apparently more prevalent than macrotroponin T, study authors suggested implications for interpreting cTnI results in real-world practice.

"Despite the consistent high prognostic value of cTnI demonstrated in numerous studies and individual participant meta-analyses, misclassification of risk based on high concentrations due to the presence of cTnI autoantibodies has been recognized as a potential problem. The current findings suggest that accounting for the presence of macro-cTnI may enhance the prognostic value of cTnI by reducing the extent of risk misclassification," they wrote.

Omland's team based the study on 3,703 community dwellers (median age 64 years, 49% women) participating in the Akershus Cardiac Examination 1950 Study.

Serum cTnI was initially analyzed using the ARCHITECT STAT high-sensitivity (hs) assay; the same samples were used to measure cTnT on a Cobas e801 using the STAT hs-troponin T assay. Investigators then sought samples where cTnI exceeded 10 ng/L (approximately corresponding to the study-specific 95th percentile) for subsequent detection of macro-cTnI.

Out of 108 people with such high cTnI, 81% met criteria for having macro-cTnI. Participants with original cTnI concentration <5 ng/L (n=3,256) or 5-10 ng/L (n=267) were the control groups.

The investigators found that people with high cTnI and prevalent macro-cTnI tended to have lower cTnT concentrations (9.0 vs 19.0 ng/L without macro-cTnI, P<0.001).

Beyond that, there were no significant between-group differences for age, sex, kidney function, C-reactive protein concentrations, use of cardioactive medications, prior cardiovascular disease, or risk factors at baseline.

The study's primary endpoint covered a composite of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, heart failure, coronary revascularization, and cardiovascular mortality.

Compared with people with cTnI levels under 5 ng/L, those with a high cTnI and macro-cTnI turned out not to be at significantly greater cardiovascular risk (7.2% vs 6.8%; adjusted HR 0.7, 95% CI 0.3-1.6).

Study authors cautioned that the study was limited by the complexity of the macrotroponin detection method used and the moderate number of participants with cTnI >10 ng/L, among other caveats.

"It remains unknown whether assay interference or delayed clearance of macrotroponin causes higher cTnI levels in those classified as macro-cTnI positive," Omland and colleagues added. "As such, these observations should be regarded as preliminary and hypothesis-generating, requiring validation in larger, more diverse, and higher-risk study populations."

#5600. Opinion: The problem with ‘zero tolerance for bad behavior’ signs at hospitals

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

By Autumn Fiester, Aliza Narva, and Stacy C. Smith

Fiester is professor of medical ethics and health policy at the University of Pennsylvania’s Perelman School of Medicine and director of the Penn Program in Clinical Conflict Management. Narva is the director of ethics at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania. Smith is a registered nurse, certified health care ethics consultant, and qualitative researcher.

Enter any hospital today and you’ll see signs warning patients and visitors that abusive language, disruptive behavior, or aggression will not be tolerated. Some threaten removal from the facility. Others warn that security or police may be called for infractions. Almost all of them declare “zero tolerance” for any of these behaviors.

The motivation behind these signs is understandable. Workplace violence against health care workers is a serious problem in U.S. hospitals, with research demonstrating an increase in frequency over the past five years.

In response to this widespread problem, both state governments and hospitals have made a concerted effort to demonstrate that they are taking this problem seriously. They have enacted a range of anti-violence measures that include reporting systems, de-escalation training programs, weapon-detection portals, increased security presence, and posted behavior signs.  Our own health system has implemented similar measures.

While these efforts are laudable in intent, not all of them are evidence-based with demonstrable efficacy in curtailing workplace violence. That includes the now-ubiquitous posted hospital behavior signs. Multiple studies that have tested these signs do not deter patients or families from committing acts of violence or reduce the frequency of physical threats.

If posted hospital behavior signs were merely ineffective at reducing workplace violence, they would be pointless, but not harmful.

But we believe that behavior signage is more problematic than it appears. The content of the signs sends clear messages to patients and families about their tenuous status and value in the institution. These signs telegraph to patients and their loved ones that they are on notice, warned that their care can be withheld and their behavior policed — even punished. In the urgency to reduce violence against health care workers, hospitals have failed to consider the message these signs communicate and whether that message aligns or conflicts with the core values of medicine: trust, care, compassion.

In our review of posted behavior signs, we found that they target only patient and visitor conduct. They rattle off a list of patient and family “do nots,” the hospital’s mechanisms of behavior enforcement, and the dire consequences of behavioral infractions. Even when the signs give a nominal nod to the institution’s commitment to reciprocal expectations for respectful communication between patients and the clinical staff, the list of “do nots” applies only to patients and families. They list no parallel behavioral standards for nurses or physicians. That makes behavior signs ignore the relational aspect of conflict. Research on lapses in clinical professionalism points to a more nuanced explanation for some of the challenging behaviors exhibited by families and patients. The Joint Commission has even named such clinical behavior as one of the causes of violence against health care workers.

Behavior signs also display from a type of institutional amnesia, forgetting why patients and families have come to the hospital in the first place: They are in pain, anxious, frightened, grieving. They may have or soon receive a life-altering diagnosis or a heartbreaking prognosis. They are vulnerable. Is this a group of people who should receive stern warnings and threats of removal as they enter the building?

When signs espouse “zero tolerance” for “noncompliant,” “disrespectful,” or “demanding” behavior, they signal to patients and their families that raising concerns about their care can be interpreted as misconduct. In a setting where patients and families already feel profound vulnerability, voicing a complaint about their clinical care can feel too risky.

That silence risks patient safety. Data show that patient and family feedback can reveal genuine safety concerns and quality issues that would fly under the radar if they remained unvoiced. Without patients and families feeling welcome to express concerns, hospitals can miss the exact information that would improve patient care and prevent patient harm.

Hospitals do not have to choose between protecting hospital staff and preserving patient/family trust in the institution.

Imagine signs that convey not threats, but shared expectations and a willingness to help when things go wrong:

“Our staff is here to help you during what may be one of the most difficult days of your life. We ask everyone, including staff, patients, and families, to treat one another with respect. If something is not going well, please let us know so we can help resolve it.”

Such messages still make clear that violence will not be tolerated. But they also clearly convey that health care is a partnership, that the experience of illness can be challenging, and that civility helps everyone. They express behavioral standards, while also indicating that the hospital’s response to challenging interactions is to help, not punish. Some hospital systems have already replaced their “zero tolerance” signs with civility signs that project care and concern.

Protecting health care workers from violence must continue to be an institutional priority, but that effort requires evidence-based prevention programs, including efforts to understand and address the root causes of conflict.

Messages about patient, family, and clinical staff behavior can be delivered in a way that acknowledges the concerns of hospital employees while also preserving patients’ and families’ sense of belonging and their ability to ask hard questions, voice concerns, and participate fully in their care.

The words we post on hospital walls must communicate more than rules. They must communicate medicine’s values.

Autumn Fiester, Ph.D., is professor of medical ethics and health policy at the University of Pennsylvania’s Perelman School of Medicine and director of the Penn Program in Clinical Conflict Management. Aliza Narva, J.D., R.N., is the director of ethics at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, where she leads the hospital’s ethics committee, ethics consultation service, ethics education initiatives, and nurse leader ethics fellowship. Stacy C. Smith, Ph.D., R.N., is a registered nurse, certified health care ethics consultant, and qualitative researcher whose work focuses on conflict and communication at the bedside.

Have an opinion on this essay? Submit a letter to the editor.

The smartest thinkers in life sciences on what's happening — and what's to come

Reporting from the frontiers of health and medicine

#5599. EXCLUSIVE: Betsey Johnson Relists California Home With Over $100K Price Cut

Betsey Johnson has relisted her California property with an $140,000 price cut—putting its new asking price at $6.8 million.

The iconic fashion designer, 84, snapped up the 4,300-square-foot abode on April 11, 2025, paying $6.85 million.

Just over a year later, on July 27, 2026, Johnson listed the home for $7.5 million. By Sept. 15, the price had been slashed by half a million dollars, asking $6.99 million. A month later, on Oct. 17, the listing was removed.

Now, the home has once again appeared on the selling block with a reduced asking price, being listed with Chris Cortazzo of Compass.

The property, which was built in 1957, boasts five bedrooms and 4.5 bathrooms.

"Tucked behind gates on Eldorado Meadow Road, this single-level contemporary residence enjoys an exceptional vantage point within Hidden Hills, with expansive views of rolling hills, distant mountain ridgelines, and beautiful open meadows," the listing reads.

Surrounded by lush greenery, the home boasts a spa-inspired pool and plenty of space for entertaining.

Upon entering the home, guests are greeted with an expansive floor plan and a chic lounging area that flows effortlessly into the dining space and opens up to the outdoors.

The kitchen is surely the crown jewel of the property as it comes complete with a black marble island and state-of-the-art appliances.

"Inside, wide-plank wood floors and exposed beams carry through the open living and dining areas. A glass-front wine display sits just off the entry, while a wall of pocketing glass opens the living room to the pool and mountains beyond. French doors beside the dining area lead to a covered terrace. In the kitchen, richly veined black marble extends from the backsplash to a waterfall island with counter seating. Woven pendants, wood cabinetry, a six-burner range with double ovens, Thermador appliances, and a concealed bar complete the space," adds the listing.

The bedrooms are the perfect place to relax and boast enough space for a queen-sized bed.

The primary bathroom features a large soaking tub and a glass-enclosed shower.

The property also comes complete with a large walk-in closet and an office space.

"Beyond, the primary suite occupies nearly an entire wing. A fireplace and white-painted beams frame the bedroom, and a sunlit sitting area opens directly to the poolside deck. The dressing room is lined with built-in cabinetry. In the bath, slatted wood walls complement a floating black stone double vanity, a glass-enclosed shower with dual showerheads, and a freestanding soaking tub set against a broad garden-facing window," the description continues.

Moving outside, the grounds offer a lovely area to kick back and enjoy the California sunshine.

"A poolside sun deck and outdoor shower complete the garden. Additional amenities include integrated audio, home automation, a two-car garage, and gated driveway parking for approximately 10 to 12 vehicles," adds the listing.

The designer's real estate portfolio has an impressive track record.

In 2019, the designer—who had previously spent 55 years living in New York City—sold her one-of-a-kind pink mobile home for $1.95 million.

The Malibu dwelling was located in Paradise Cove Mobile Home Park, which is considered to be one of the most famous and luxurious trailer parks in the country.

The picturesque community of 270 homes has attracted many notable residents, including Sarah Paulson, Stevie Nicks, and Pamela Anderson.

Before offloading the mobile home, Johnson spent over $500,000 turning it into a playful wonderland decorated with countless bohemian prints, florals, and electric colors. There was even a fully functional outdoor tub.

“I would like people to think of this as a funny little museum,” she told People magazine in 2018, referring to the expansive collection of antiques and vintage finds she had displayed in the home.

The mobile home had two bedrooms and two bathrooms, and plenty of room for her daughter, Lulu Johnson, 41, and two grandchildren, Layla and Ella, who reportedly also lived in Malibu, visiting frequently.

“I’ve made lots of mistakes with boyfriends and husbands,” said Johnson, who has been married three times. “I don’t think I’ve made more than two mistakes with my houses, purchases for my houses, or the clothes in my closet.”

It wasn’t long before Johnson would find herself in yet another pink mobile home in Malibu, moving into a 2,300-square-foot home in the gated Point Dume Club.

“I love the idea that, with a trailer park, you’re in a kind of community,” she told the New York Times Style Magazine in 2021. “At my age, if I fall down in the middle of the street, I want someone to go, ‘Hey! What’s that girl doing in the middle of the street?’”

Soon after moving in, Johnson papered the walls with vintage wallpaper that perfectly matched the floral print from her childhood home.

Pink homes are somewhat of a tradition for Johnson, who famously lived in a bubblegum pink loft in Manhattan in the 1980s—the photos of which still regularly circulate on blogs and social media accounts dedicated to whimsical design.

And although the exterior is not pink, Johnson does also have a four-bedroom, six-bathroom vacation home in Guerrero, Mexico, where her half-punk, half-ballerina touch can be found in every room.

According to Elle Decor, the property—aptly named “Betseyvilla”—was previously offered as a rental through Airbnb, although the listing appears to no longer be available.

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.
